With poder you also ask for permission or a favour: “¿Puedo salir a las dos?”, “¿Puedes reservar el hotel?”. With querer you invite: “¿Quieres venir a la playa?”.
Laura has little money: she cannot pay for an expensive hotel.
For the flight, Gabriel has to bring his ID card.
Laura talks to her boss: “Can I leave early on Friday?”
Laura wants to go to the islands.
Laura is going to go to the islands on Saturday.
I don’t want to pay for the boat.
I can’t pay for the boat.
I don’t have to pay for the boat today.
“No tengo que” means it is not necessary. To say that something is impossible or not allowed, use “no puedo”: “I can’t take much water on the plane”.
Monday is a public holiday: Laura doesn’t have to work.
“Gabriel quiere ir a la playa” means…
Laura has no money for the boat. She says: “I can’t go to the islands”.
Which one is correct?
Julio, I need help. Gabriel and I want to travel to Cartagena on the long weekend.
Great! When can you leave?
I can leave on Friday morning, but Gabriel has to work until two.
Then you have to take the six p.m. flight. And how much money can you spend?
Not much. We can only pay for a small hotel. But I want to see the Rosario Islands!
Hmm… The boat to the islands is expensive. And for the boat, you have to book this week.
This week? I can’t decide today: I have to talk to Gabriel.
Of course. Some good news: you don’t have to come back on Sunday. Monday is a public holiday.
Perfect! Then on Sunday we can go to the beach all day.
Yes. And on Monday morning you are going to fly back to Bogotá on the eleven o’clock flight.
Thanks, Julio. I’ll talk to Gabriel tonight. I want to go to the islands!
Why can’t they take a flight on Friday morning?
Why doesn’t Laura decide about the islands today?
Do they have to come back on Sunday?
Mrs Ríos, can I leave at two on Friday?
Yes, you can leave at two.
Do you want to go to the islands on Saturday?
Laura and Gabriel have to book the hotel today.
We cannot spend much money.
I want to see the islands.
Can you book the hotel?
We can’t pay for an expensive hotel.
Why does Julio send the message?
When can they pay for the hotel?
By when do they have to book the boat?
What time do they have to be at the airport?
What does Laura have to bring?
want to
can / can’t
have to · don’t have to
Conjugated verb + infinitive. Querer and poder go straight to the infinitive; tener needs “que”. And careful: “no puedo” = impossible; “no tengo que” = not necessary.
On Friday Gabriel has to work until two.
Laura really likes the sea: she wants to see the islands.
I have no money: I can’t pay for the boat.
Can you all travel on Monday?
Tomorrow is a holiday: I don’t have to go to the office. Great!
Sara, a colleague of Laura’s, also wants to travel: to Medellín, with her mother. Write one sentence for each idea.

You can now say what you want, can and have to do with a verb + infinitive. In class 041 you meet another two-verb combination: estar + gerund, to say what you are doing right now. “I am booking the hotel right now”.
It is Saturday, six in the evening. Sofía calls her friend Pablo: “What are you doing?”. Pablo answers: “I am cooking right now”. Today you learn to say what is happening at this moment.
I work every day, Monday to Friday.
I am not working today. Right now I am cooking.
“Ahora estoy cocinando” is about…
“Trabajo todos los días” is about…
Sofía asks about this moment. What does she say?
to be + -ing: what is happening now
I am cooking a soup now.
Mario is listening to the radio.
Sofía and her friends are waiting at the cinema.
What are you doing, Pablo?
Irene and Pablo are cooking.
Which piece changes with the person?
To make the gerund, take off -ar, -er or -ir and add -ando or -iendo. There are only two endings.
“Le + iendo” is written leyendo: an i between two vowels becomes y. “Dormir” changes o to u: durmiendo.
to speak → speaking
to drink → drinking
to read → reading
to sleep → sleeping
Sometimes people use the present for now: “¿Qué haces?” — “Cocino”. That is correct. But to say clearly that the action is in progress, use estar + gerund: “Estoy cocinando”.
On Saturdays Pablo rests at home.
Shh… Irene is sleeping right now.
Irene works at night at the hospital. She is a nurse.
I am listening to the radio now.
We are eating.
Hi, Pablo! What are you doing?
Hi, Sofía. Right now I am cooking a vegetable soup.
Yum! Aren’t you working today?
No. I work Monday to Friday. On Saturdays I rest.
And Irene? Is she at home?
Yes, but she is sleeping. She works nights at the hospital.
Oh, of course. I can hear another voice. Who is talking?
It is the radio. My brother Mario is reading on the sofa and listening to the football.
Listen, Lucas, Ana and I are going to the cinema at eight. Are you coming?
I can’t today, sorry. My parents are coming for dinner at eight.
OK, another day. Enjoy your meal!
What is Pablo doing?
Why is Irene sleeping?
What is Mario doing?
I am making rice for my parents now.
Irene is sleeping in her room.
Mario is reading a novel.
Sofía, Lucas and Ana are waiting in line.
And you, Sofía? What are you doing now?
Irene is sleeping now.
Mario is reading a book.
We are watching the film.
I work every day, but today I am resting.
Where is Sofía?
What is Sofía doing?
What is Lucas doing?
What is the weather like?
What time does the film start today?
to be + -ing: happening now
present: what you usually do
two special forms to remember

Two pieces, always: estar conjugated + gerund (-ando, -iendo). Only estar changes; the gerund never does. Routine goes in the present: “Trabajo todos los días”; what is happening now goes with estar + gerund: “Estoy trabajando ahora”.
Shh… the neighbours’ baby is sleeping.
Right now Ana and I are having a coffee.
Lucas works in an office every day.
What are you reading now?
My friends are eating in a restaurant.
It is Monday morning. Pablo is at work and his boss, Elena, phones: “What is everyone doing?”. Write Pablo’s answers.

You can now say what you are doing: “Estoy cocinando la sopa”. In class 042 you learn not to repeat those things, with lo, la, los, las: “¿La sopa? La estoy cocinando”. It is the natural next step to speak more fluently.

It is Monday morning at a small design company. Marta, the coordinator, finds a note from her boss, Elena: “Ana buys bread today”. On Friday there is a lunch with clients at the office, and the team needs to know who does what and when.
Ana buys bread today.
What does Ana buy?
Ana does not buy cheese.
“Ana compra pan hoy” is…
“¿Qué compra Ana?” asks about…
In “Ana no compra queso”, “no” goes…
Who does what, and when?
Elena is away on a trip this week.
Marta and Elena work at a design company.
I buy the coffee on Mondays.
Ana buys bread today. = Today Ana buys bread.
Ana calls Diego. ≠ Diego calls Ana.
In “Ana llama a Diego”, Ana does the action and Diego receives it. The person after “a” receives the call.
“Hoy Ana compra pan” means…
“Diego llama a Ana”: who is calling?
Today Elena and Ana make the coffee.
Yes / no, or a piece of information?
Is Ana buying bread today? — Yes.
The same question: the verb can also go first.
What does Ana buy? — Bread.
Who buys bread? — Ana.
When does Ana buy bread? — Today.
Who buys bread?
When does Ana buy bread?
In a yes / no question, your voice goes up at the end. In a statement, it goes down. In writing, Spanish uses two marks: ¿ at the start and ? at the end.
Marta wants to know the person. What does she ask?
Which one is correct?
“¿Ana compra pan hoy?” A possible answer:
Where does “no” go?
Today Elena is not working at the office: she is away.
The cheese? Ana does not buy it.
“Is Ana buying cheese?” “No, she isn’t buying cheese.”
Elena is not working this week.
The bread? Ana is not buying it tomorrow: she is buying it today.
“Is Elena at the office?” “No, she isn’t.”
Good morning, team. There is a note from Elena, but it has a coffee stain. Who is calling the restaurant on Wednesday?
Me. Elena isn’t here this week, so I’m calling the restaurant.
Thanks, Diego. Ana, are you buying the bread today?
Yes, I’m buying the bread today. But I’m not buying the cheese.
The note says: “Lucía does not prepare the room”. So what do I prepare?
You prepare the drinks, Lucía. I prepare the room on Thursday.
Perfect. And the flowers? When is Raúl buying the flowers?
It isn’t clear. Is Raúl buying the flowers on Thursday or on Friday?
Not on Thursday. Raúl doesn’t work on Thursdays.
Then he buys them on Friday morning. Who is talking to Raúl today?
I’ll talk to him at eleven. See you later!
Who is calling the restaurant?
What does Marta prepare on Thursday?
Who is talking to Raúl today?
What does Marta ask?
When does Diego call the restaurant?
On Friday Raúl and Ana arrive early at the office.
“Does Raúl work on Thursdays?” “No, he doesn’t work on Thursdays.”
Raúl buys flowers on Friday.
Where do the clients eat?
Diego does not work on Monday.
What does Lucía prepare?
Why does Elena call?
When does Ana buy the bread?
Why does Raúl buy the flowers on Friday?
How many clients arrive on Friday?
What does Elena ask at the end?
statement: the time phrase can move, the meaning stays
question: yes / no, or a piece of information
negative: “no” right before the verb
First who, then the verb. In a question with qué, quién or cuándo, the verb comes right after the question word. And “no” always goes before the verb: “Ana no compra pan”, never “compra no”.
Diego does not work on Tuesday.
Who closes the office? — Marta.
What is Lucía preparing for the lunch?
On Friday the clients arrive at one.
Which one is written correctly?
It is Saturday. On Lucía’s fridge there is a note: “My brother cooks on Sunday”. Sara, her flatmate, does not quite understand the note and asks questions. Write Sara’s sentences.

You can now order a sentence, ask with qué, quién or cuándo, and say no with “no”. In class 044 you put all of A1 together (ser, estar, hay, articles, possessives) to describe a place and ask for useful information: “¿Dónde está tu habitación?”. It is the natural next step: using these sentences in a complete conversation.

It is Sunday afternoon. Carmen is travelling for a week for work. Her friend Daniel is going to look after her flat and her cat, Luna. Carmen shows him around: “This is my home”. Daniel asks: “Where is my room?”. Today you put together everything you know to describe a place and ask for information.
The living room is small and bright.
In the living room there is a sofa and two lamps.
The sofa is next to the window.
“En el salón hay un sofá” tells you…
“El sofá está junto a la ventana” tells you…
Daniel wants to know what the living room is like. What does Carmen say?
there is / there are: something new, or how many
There is a small table on the terrace.
There are two cupboards in the hallway.
There is fruit and milk in the fridge.
to be (location): where a known thing is
The table is on the terrace.
My books are in that cupboard.
Luna is in the kitchen.
There is a plant in the hallway.
The plant is next to the door.
We often use both forms, one after the other. First you introduce the thing with hay; then the thing is known and you say where it is: “There are two chairs; they are next to my table”.
There are two towels in the bathroom. They are in the cupboard.
The kitchen is small, but it is very nice.
Daniel is looking for the bathroom. What does he ask?
With a non-specific thing (any one) you can say “¿Dónde hay una farmacia?”. With a specific thing you say “¿Dónde está la farmacia?”. Both questions are correct.
Daniel wants to know the number of blankets. What does he ask?
Daniel sees a box and does not know what it is. What does he ask?
My keys are on the table.
There is a very comfortable sofa here.
Your shoes are under the bed.
Welcome, Daniel! This is my home. It is small, but very bright.
It is very nice! Where is my room?
It is at the end of the hallway, on the left. There is a big bed and a wardrobe.
Perfect. Are there any towels?
Yes, they are in the bathroom cupboard. And this is the kitchen: there are two chairs; they are next to my table.
And my key? How many keys are there?
There are two: one for me and one for you. Your key is on that table, next to the door.
And Luna? I can’t see Luna.
Look, she is under the sofa. She is very calm.
One more question: what is this?
It is the wifi router. Oh, the password! I don’t know where it is… I will send you a message tomorrow.
Where is Daniel’s room?
Where is Daniel’s key?
What does Carmen not know?
There is a new shower in the bathroom.
Where are the cups?
The kitchen chairs are made of wood.
This cupboard is for your clothes.
And your books? Where are they?
There are two lamps; they are in the living room.
Where is my suitcase?
This room is very quiet.
How many pictures are there in the hallway?
Why does Carmen send the message?
Where is Luna’s food?
Where is the wifi password?
What is the blanket like?
Who is Rosa?
what it is, what it is like, whose
there is / there are: new things, how many
where a specific thing is
asking for useful information
Look at the word before the noun. Un, una, dos, muchos → hay: “Hay dos sillas”. El, la, mi, tu, este → está / están: “Las sillas están junto a mi mesa”. And to describe, ser: “La mesa es grande”.
There is a very good bakery on my street.
The bakery is next to the bank.
How many windows are there in your room?
My glasses are on top of that book.
Whose is that suitcase over there?
Now Daniel is in a hotel. He has questions for the receptionist. Write Daniel’s questions.

You can now describe a place in the present: what it is, what there is and where each thing is. In class 045 you take one more step and talk about your experiences: “I have been to Lima”, “Have you visited Mexico?”. It is the natural next step: from describing what you see now to telling what you have lived.

It is Friday, five in the afternoon, at the neighbourhood cultural centre. A photo exhibition opens tomorrow. Nuria, the coordinator, checks the task list: “I have opened the door and I have written to Ana”. To say what you have already done today you need haber + past participle.
Lucía has cleaned the room.
I have opened the door and I have written to Ana.
“He escrito a Ana” is about…
Which participle follows the normal rule?
how to make a regular past participle
Raúl has called the print shop.
We have sold twenty tickets.
Have you received Ana’s parcel?
Óscar has already left for the bank.
to prepare → prepared
to live → lived
Lucía and Raúl have asked for boxes for the photos.
Verbs from the same family follow the same pattern: describir → descrito, devolver → devuelto, deshacer → deshecho. If you know escrito, vuelto and hecho, you already know these.
to put → put
to come back → come back
to say → said
I have written to Ana today.
I wrote to Ana yesterday.
In many Latin American countries people also say “Hoy escribí a Ana”. In Spain “Hoy he escrito” is more common. Both are correct; today you practise haber + participle.
This morning Óscar has switched on the lights in the room.
Which sentence tells about a task already done today?
You will also see “La sala está abierta”. With estar, the participle works as an adjective and changes. With haber it never changes.
Nuria has written the invitations.
The girls have opened the windows.
Right, team, let’s check the list. Lucía, have you opened the big room?
Yes, I opened it at nine and I have cleaned the floor.
Perfect. Raúl, what about the posters?
I have already made them. They are at the entrance.
Great! Has anyone written to Ana, the photographer?
Yes, me. Ana has answered and has said she is coming at six.
Great. And the photos? Have you put the photos on the walls yet?
Not yet. But we have prepared the frames.
Well… almost all of them. I have broken a frame. Sorry!
No problem. This morning I went to the shop and bought two more frames.
Problem solved! By the way, has anyone seen my keys?
Yes, you have put them in the poster box.
What has Lucía done today?
Which task is not done yet?
Why has Raúl gone to the shop?
This afternoon I have made the exhibition leaflets.
Ana is already back from her trip.
We have already put the chairs in the room.
Lucía has written a message to the press.
Óscar, have you seen the centre’s new website?
Ana has seen the photos.
We haven’t written the email yet.
Who has broken the mug?
Why does Nuria call?
Who has opened the room?
What has Nuria done?
What has happened with the frame?
What haven’t they done yet?
the rule for almost every verb
forms you learn by heart
a finished time: next class
Haber changes with the person; the participle never changes. First think: is it one of the eight? If not, -ado or -ido. Escrito, never “escribido”.
This week my neighbours have written two letters to the town hall.
Who has opened the window? It is cold.
Today my son has done his homework on his own.
This month I have sold three books at the market.
Have you seen the new exhibition yet?
It is Sunday and Lucía is tidying the flat with her flatmate, Hugo. Her mother calls: “What have you done today?”. Write the answers.

You can now say what you have done today: “He escrito a Ana”. In class 047 you learn to tell what happened yesterday or last week with the preterite: “Ayer escribí a Ana”. You have already seen it in the violet examples; it is the natural next step to talk about a finished past.

It is Monday. Clara arrives at the office and her colleague Óscar asks: “How was your visit to Oaxaca?”. Clara answers: “I went by bus, but the bus had a problem”. The visit is over. Today you learn the most frequent irregular past verbs.
Today I go to the office by metro.
On Friday I went to Oaxaca by bus.
“El viernes fui a Oaxaca” is about…
“Fui” is the past of…
Óscar asks about last weekend. What does he say?
What happened? What did you do?
The bus had a problem on the road.
Marta was at the bus station for two hours.
I couldn’t get into the museum.
On Sunday I made a soup and Marta said: “Thank you!”.
to have, I, on Saturday → I had
to do / make, she, yesterday → she did / made
Where did she go? How was it?
Clara went to Oaxaca on Friday.
The trip was very long.
I went to the market alone.
In the end, it was a nice visit.
“El fin de semana fue difícil”. Here “fue” is…
“Marta fue a la terminal”. Here “fue” is…

In regular verbs the stress falls on the ending: llegué, comí, salió. In these irregular verbs it falls on the stem: tuve, hizo, pudo. That is why they have no written accent. Fui and fue don’t either: they have only one syllable.
Today I am at home. I work from here.
Last night I couldn’t sleep well.
On Friday Clara said to Óscar: “I am off to Oaxaca”.
On Sunday I packed my suitcase early.
Yesterday Marta was at the doctor’s for an hour.
Hi, Clara! How was Oaxaca? What did you do?
Phew, it was a weekend full of surprises.
Why? What happened?
On Friday I went by bus, but the bus had a problem on the road. I arrived at eleven at night!
How awful! And Marta?
She was at the bus station for two hours. And on Saturday she had a fever and couldn’t leave the house.
So you were on your own all Saturday?
Yes. In the morning I went to the market. In the afternoon I couldn’t get into the museum: I didn’t book.
What bad luck! And on Sunday?
On Sunday I made a soup for Marta. She said: “You are the best friend in the world!”.
So, in the end, was it a good visit?
Yes, very nice. But now I am very sleepy. Today I am going home early.
Why did Clara arrive late in Oaxaca?
Why couldn’t Clara get into the museum?
What did Clara do on Sunday?
On Friday I went to the bus station at five in the afternoon.
It was very hot on Saturday.
I didn’t have time to make the booking.
Marta said: “How delicious!”.
On Friday I went to Oaxaca.
The bus had a problem.
Marta couldn’t leave the house.
Clara said that it was a difficult trip.
What is the main idea?
What did the doctor say?
What did Marta find on the sofa?
Why couldn’t she call Clara?
What did Marta make for her sister yesterday?
new stem, -e / -o, no written accent
same forms, two verbs: to go / to be
present: today, now; the indefinido is for what is finished

Six very frequent verbs change their stem in the past: hic-, tuv-, estuv-, pud-, dij- and fu-. “I” ends in -e and “he / she” in -o, with no written accent: hice, hizo. Never “hací” or “tení”. And with today and now, the present: “Ayer fui, hoy voy”.
Last week my boss went to Lima for work.
Last night I didn’t make dinner: I ordered a pizza.
The concert was amazing.
Yesterday my neighbours weren’t at home and I couldn’t talk to them.
Today I have a lot of work, but yesterday I had a quiet day.
A month later, Óscar visits his parents in Monterrey. On Monday, Clara asks: “How was the visit?”. Write Óscar’s sentences.

You can now tell what happened: “Fui a Oaxaca”, “Marta tuvo fiebre”. In class 049 you learn the imperfect to describe how things were and what you always did in the past: “As a girl, I went to Oaxaca every summer”. It is the natural next step: first the events, then the background of the story.

Carmen Ortega lives on Colón Street. Yesterday she saw a small accident from the bus stop. This morning Carmen was sleeping when the phone rang: it was Officer Prado, from the local police. She wanted to talk about the accident. Today you learn to tell a story with two past tenses: the scene and the events.
Carmen was sleeping… (the background: what was going on)
…when the phone rang. (the event: the story moves on)
“Carmen dormía” is about…
“Sonó el teléfono” is about…
Then Carmen answered the phone and talked to the officer.
What was the scene like? What was going on?
It was half past eight in the morning.
It was raining a little and there was a lot of traffic.
A young man was cycling along the street.
What happened? And then?
Suddenly, a taxi came out of a garage.
The young man braked and fell.
Carmen called emergency services.
There were a lot of people at the stop.
A taxi came out of a garage.

Look at these two sentences: “When the ambulance arrived, Diego was sitting down” (the scene) and “When the ambulance arrived, Diego stood up” (the next event). Both are correct. The word “cuando” does not choose the tense: what you want to say does.
On Saturday it rained all afternoon and I didn’t leave the house.
It was raining when Carmen left home, so she took an umbrella.
When the ambulance arrived, Diego was sitting on the ground.
Yesterday there was an accident on my street.
It was early. It was half past eight.

An accident, a storm, a party, a power cut: these are things that happen. To say they happened, use haber in the indefinido: “Ayer hubo un accidente”. “Era” is the verb ser: use it for the time (“eran las ocho”) or to describe (“el chico era joven”).
Yesterday there was an accident on Colón Street.
When I went out, there was a lot of traffic in the street.
He was young, about twenty years old.
It was nine o’clock when the officer arrived.
Carmen was reading the newspaper and suddenly she heard a loud noise.
Good morning, Mrs Ortega. Yesterday morning there was an accident on your street. Did you see it?
Yes, I saw it all. It was half past eight. I was waiting for the bus at the stop.
What was the weather like?
It was raining a little and there was a lot of traffic. The road was wet.
I see. And what happened?
A young man was cycling along the street. Suddenly, a taxi came out of a garage.
Did the taxi hit the bicycle?
No. The young man braked very hard, but with the wet road he fell.
And what did you do?
I ran to help the young man and called emergency services. The taxi driver stopped too.
How was the young man?
His knee was hurt, but he was calm. When the ambulance arrived, he was already talking on the phone with his sister.
Where was Carmen at half past eight?
Why did the young man fall?
What was the young man doing when the ambulance arrived?
At half past eight there was a lot of traffic on Colón Street.
At eight thirty-five there was an accident on the corner.
The cyclist was wearing a blue helmet and a black jacket.
The taxi driver got out of the car and helped the young man.
Diego was at the hospital for two hours and then went back home.
It was raining when Carmen left home.
Yesterday there was an accident on the corner.
It was seven o’clock when the phone rang.
Diego was going to work when he fell.
What is the main idea?
Where was Diego going?
What was the scene like?
What is wrong with Diego now?
What does Diego want to do next week?
the scene: time, weather, place, what was going on
the events that move the story on
long, but with an end: indefinido

A story has two layers. The scene (imperfect): “Eran las ocho, llovía, yo esperaba el autobús”. The events (indefinido): “De repente, un taxi salió y el chico se cayó”. An accident happens: “hubo un accidente”, never “era un accidente”. And “cuando” does not decide: you do.
Last night there was a very strong storm in the city.
While I was making dinner, the doorbell rang.
It was eleven at night and the street was empty.
On Sunday it rained all day, so we didn’t go out.
When the technician arrived, the lift was already working.
A week later, there is a power cut in the local library. Carmen was there. Join the sentences and tell what happened: scene + event.

You can now tell a story with a scene and events: “Llovía cuando salí”, “Hubo un accidente”. In class 051 you look at another past-tense contrast: “Hoy he hablado con Ana” and “Hoy hablé con Ana”. Both are correct: it depends on the region. It is the natural next step: now that you choose well between background and event, you learn how people talk about the recent past in Spain and in Latin America.

It is six in the evening at a language school in Madrid. Lucía is a teacher from Puebla, in Mexico. Pablo is a teacher from Madrid. They both talk about their day. Pablo says: “I’ve talked to Ana today”. Lucía says: “I talked to Ana today”. Who is right? Both of them.
I’ve talked to Ana today.
I talked to Ana today.
Which sentence is correct?
“He hablado” is…
Why does Lucía say “hoy hablé”?
What have you done today?
I’ve had three classes this morning.
Pablo has had lunch with his students.
Have you seen Ana today?
What did you do today?
This morning I had three classes.
Lucía had lunch with Ana at noon.
Did you see Ana today?
“Esta mañana desayuné en casa”. When did it happen?
Pablo asks Lucía if she has eaten. What does Pablo, from Madrid, usually say?

There is variation inside Spain too: in the Canary Islands and parts of Galicia and Asturias, the indefinido is frequent for today. And in some areas of Latin America, such as the Andes, the perfecto is more frequent. That is why we say “frequent in”, not “always”.
Last night Pablo got home very late.
Lucía, in Puebla, talks about today: “I worked a lot today”.
Two educated standards of Spanish. Both are correct.
“He comí” mixes both forms. With “ayer”, the standard in every variety is “comí”.
A teacher from Guadalajara, Mexico, says: “Hoy terminé el libro”.
A student writes: “Esta mañana he escribí un correo”.
A man from Valladolid says: “Este año he viajado poco”.
Last Monday I had a difficult exam.
Someone says: “Hoy comí tacos”. You answer…
Phew, what a day! How was yours, Lucía?
Good, but long. This morning I had three classes and at noon I had lunch with Ana.
Great! I have talked to Ana today too. We have planned Friday’s trip.
Hey, Pablo, a question. You say “he hablado” and I say “hablé”. Am I saying it wrong?
No, not at all! Both forms are correct. In Madrid, for today, we mostly say “he hablado”.
And in Puebla we say “hoy hablé”. My mother always asks me: “Have you eaten yet, sweetie?”.
How lovely! My mother says “¿Ya has comido?”. It is the same question.
And for yesterday? Do you say “ayer he hablado”?
No, not that. For yesterday I say “hablé” too. For example: yesterday I went to the cinema and got home late.
So, with yesterday, we both say the same thing. How easy!
Exactly. And what have you done this afternoon? Oops, sorry: what did you do?
Both questions are fine! I marked exams and wrote to my family.
What does Lucía ask Pablo?
What does Pablo answer?
Which form does Pablo use for yesterday?
I’ve written an email to Ana this morning.
Today I talked a lot with my students.
Last Monday Ana made a cake for everyone.
Which sentence is correct to talk about today?
Pablo has written to the students this afternoon.
Lucía marked the exams today.
Have you finished the exams yet?
Yesterday we went to the cinema.
What is the main idea?
Who made the museum booking?
How many students have answered?
What did Pablo forget yesterday?
frequent in much of Spain
frequent in Mexico and much of Latin America
in every variety

For today, both forms are correct: “Hoy he comido” is frequent in Spain and “Hoy comí” in Mexico and much of Latin America. It is not a mistake: it is a variety. For yesterday, everyone uses the indefinido. And we never mix: no “he comí”, and no “hable” without the accent.
Last night my neighbours had a party.
A journalist from Mexico City: “Today I talked to the museum director”.
A waiter from Zaragoza: “This week I have worked a lot”.
“Hoy salí temprano” is…
Last year I was in Puebla.

On Friday, after the trip, Lucía calls her mother in Puebla and Pablo calls his grandmother in Valladolid. Write their sentences: each uses their own variety for today, and both use the indefinido for yesterday.

You can now tell your day in both varieties, and you know that with “ayer” everyone uses the indefinido. Class 052, “Solía + infinitive and old habits”, comes next in the course: you learn to talk about what you used to do: “As a girl, I used to eat at my grandmother’s”. It is not published yet; in the meantime, see the course in order.

In many Latin American countries, for 8:45 people also say “Faltan quince para las nueve” (fifteen minutes to nine) or “Es un cuarto para las nueve”, and in some areas people ask “¿Qué horas son?”. These are correct regional variants: if you use them, they are fine. In this class we practise “son las nueve menos cuarto / menos quince”, which is understood everywhere.
Diego was going to work when the taxi came out.

A story has two layers. The scene (imperfect): “Eran las ocho, llovía, yo esperaba el autobús”. The events (indefinido): “De repente, un taxi salió y el chico frenó”. An accident happens: “hubo un accidente”, never “era un accidente”. And “cuando” does not decide: you do.

There is variation inside Spain too: in the Canary Islands and parts of the north-west (Galicia, Asturias, León), the indefinido is common for recent events. And in some Andean areas (for example, Bolivia, Peru or north-west Argentina), the perfecto has wider uses. That is why we say “frequent in”, not “always”.
“He comí” mixes both forms: it does not exist. “Ayer he comido” is not used in standard Spanish: with “ayer”, the normal form is “comí”.
the most common form in most of Spain
frequent in Mexico, much of Latin America and the Canary Islands
the general standard

For today, both forms are correct: “Hoy he comido” is the most common form in most of Spain and “Hoy comí” in Mexico and much of Latin America. It is not a mistake: it is a variety. For yesterday, the general standard is the indefinido. And we never mix: no “he comí”, and no “hable” without the accent.

You can now tell your day in both varieties, and you know that with “ayer” the general standard is the indefinido. Class 052, “Solía + infinitive and old habits”, comes next in the course: you learn to talk about what you used to do: “As a girl, I used to eat at my grandmother’s”. It is not published yet; in the meantime, see the course in order.

Irene Castillo works at the San Lorenzo community centre. She is preparing an exhibition of old photos: “This is how our neighbourhood used to be”. Today she talks to Rafael Ortiz, aged 79. Rafael had the bakery on the square. He looks at a photo and says: “I used to walk to work”. Today you learn to talk about old habits with solía + infinitive.
I used to walk to work. (imperfect: a past habit)
I used to walk to work. (solía says: it was my habit)
“Antes solía caminar al trabajo” means…
With “solía”, Rafael is talking about…
In those days, Rafael used to make bread every morning.
What did you usually do before? (used to + verb)
As a young man, Rafael used to walk to work.
On Sundays we used to eat at my grandmother’s house.
As a child, did you use to play in the street?
My parents used to work on Saturdays.
We used to have dinner at ten.
In those days, Rafael used to open the bakery at six.
One day in 1985 he opened at nine because there was snow.

To describe what a person or a place was like, use the plain imperfect: “Mi abuelo era alto”, “La plaza era pequeña”. With “solía” you say that something happened many times: “On Sundays, the square was usually full of children”.
As a girl, Irene used to go to the park with her father on Saturdays.
One Saturday in 1999, Irene went to the zoo with her father.
Irene’s grandfather was very tall and friendly.
And what do you usually do now?
Irene used to go by car; now she usually goes by bike.
Now Rafael usually sleeps until eight.
We didn’t use to watch TV; now we watch it a lot.
Irene didn’t use to have breakfast; now she has breakfast every day.
Now my neighbours usually buy bread at the supermarket.
As a young man, Rafael used to get up at four.
In the eighties, my uncle and aunt used to spend every summer in the countryside.
Last Monday I went to Rafael’s bakery.
Don Rafael, this photo is from 1978. Is it your bakery?
Yes, what memories! In those days I used to get up at four in the morning.
At four? And how did you use to get to the bakery?
I used to walk: twenty minutes along Calle Mayor. There were no buses at that time.
And what time did the neighbours use to come?
From seven o’clock. On Sundays, the queue went all the way to the corner.
And what did the children do?
The children used to play football on the square. Once, a ball broke my shop window.
No! And what did you do?
Nothing serious. I gave each of them a sweet roll and they went to play in another street.
And do you go past the square sometimes now?
Yes, now I usually go for a walk there in the afternoon. But my bakery is a pharmacy now.
How did Rafael use to get to the bakery?
What happened once?
What does Rafael usually do now?
In the seventies, the neighbours used to go out to the square at night with their chairs.
The newsstand man used to take the newspaper to people’s homes.
In 1982 there was a big party on the square for the neighbourhood’s 100th anniversary.
As a girl, my mother used to fetch water from the fountain on the square.
The school on Calle Mayor was very big and had a playground with trees.
I used to walk to work.
Rafael didn’t use to close on Mondays.
As a young man I used to get up at four.
What is the main idea?
Who did Mercedes use to go to the cinema with?
What did they use to buy at the kiosk?
Why didn’t her father use to go?
What happened one Sunday?
Mercedes says “celular”, as in Mexico and much of Latin America. In Spain people say “móvil”. Both words are correct.
something that was repeated in a past period; no preposition
a specific event, not a habit
today’s habit (o → ue only in the present)

“Used to” in Spanish is solía + infinitive (or the imperfect): “Antes solía caminar” = “Antes caminaba”. Never “usaba caminar”. Only soler changes; the other verb stays in the infinitive, with no “a”. For a specific day, use the indefinido: “Ayer caminé”. To describe, use the imperfect: “La plaza era pequeña”.
When I lived in Lima, I used to walk along the seafront on Sundays.
On 3 May 2015 I started my first job.
My cousins used to spend the holidays with us.
I didn’t use to have breakfast, but now I always do.
My first house was small and very bright.
Irene is preparing another part of the exhibition: work before the internet. Her colleague Hugo worked in a local office in 1990. Write his sentences with solía.
In more formal or written texts you also find “tenía la costumbre de” + infinitive (had the habit of) and “acostumbraba a” + infinitive. They mean the same as “solía”.
Solía + infinitive: no preposition. Tenía la costumbre de + infinitive: with “de”. Acostumbraba a + infinitive: usually with “a”, though it is also correct without it.
“My grandfather had the habit of reading the newspaper aloud” means…
In the exhibition text: “The neighbours used to meet on the square on Sundays”.

You can now talk about habits from another time: “Antes solía caminar al trabajo”, “Un día caminé dos horas”. Today you used “antes”, “un día” and “ahora” a lot. In class 053 you work with these time words and two new ones: “ya” and “todavía” (“I don’t walk to work any more”, “I still live here”). It is the natural next step: now you say precisely what changed and what stayed the same.

Valeria Montes lives in Guadalajara, Mexico. Today she is hosting a dinner at home for her university classmates: they studied Tourism together and graduated in 2016. It is half past seven. The food is ready, but the house is silent. Valeria texts her friend Rodrigo: “I’ve finished, but nobody has arrived yet”. Today you learn four words to place things in time: ayer, antes, ya and todavía.
I’ve already finished. (the expected action has happened)
Nobody has arrived yet. (it hasn’t happened, but she expects it)
“Ya terminé” means…
“Nobody has arrived yet”. Is Valeria expecting her friends?
Valeria asks Rodrigo at half past seven: “Have you left work yet?”
Has it happened or not?
I’ve already set the table.
The guests haven’t arrived yet.
Have you bought the ice yet? —No, not yet.
Rodrigo: “Valeria, have you put the music on yet?”
—Has Paula arrived yet? —No, not yet.
Is it still going on or not?
Valeria still works at the hotel.
Hugo doesn’t live in Zapopan any more.
Do you still play the guitar? —No, not any more.
Hugo used to live in Zapopan; now he lives downtown. Hugo no longer lives in Zapopan.
Valeria started at the hotel in 2017 and works there today. She still works at the hotel.
—Do you still have your old car? —No, not any more. I sold it last year.
Yesterday Elena called Valeria.
The friends used to see each other every week; now they hardly ever meet.

Today you use antes on its own: “Antes vivía en Zapopan” (I used to live in Zapopan). Antes can also mean “earlier”: “Hugo llegó antes”. In class 054 you will see antes de + something: “before dinner”, “before going out”.
Yesterday afternoon Valeria bought flowers for the table.
The friends used to play cards every Friday; now they hardly ever see each other.
Last night Rodrigo bought the ice for the party.
—Do you still live with your parents? —No, not any more. Now I live on my own.
It’s eight o’clock and Paula hasn’t arrived yet.
Hugo, how lovely! Come in, come in. You’re the first one: nobody has arrived yet.
Really? How strange! I always used to be late for everything.
That’s true! And do you still live in Zapopan?
No, not any more. Now I live downtown, near work. And you? Do you still work at the hotel?
Yes, I still work there, but now I’m the manager.
Congratulations! Hey, have you talked to Elena yet? Is she coming?
Yes, she’s coming. Yesterday she called me from the airport: she flew in from Madrid in the morning.
Great! And Paula?
She hasn’t answered me yet. She used to live very close to here, but now she lives in Tlaquepaque, a bit far away.
Well, can I help with anything? Have you set the table yet?
Yes, everything’s ready now. Well, I haven’t put the music on yet…
I’ll do it! We used to dance cumbia at every party, remember?
Where does Hugo live now?
Does Valeria still work at the hotel?
What hasn’t Valeria done yet?
The flowers: I already bought them this morning.
The dessert: I haven’t made it yet. I need one more hour!
Marcos no longer lives in Guadalajara: now he lives in Monterrey.
Sofía still lives in the same house, with the same dog. Nothing has changed!
Yesterday evening I bought the ice and the soft drinks.
Paula hasn’t arrived yet.
Hugo no longer lives in Zapopan.
Have you put the glasses out yet?
We used to dance cumbia every Saturday.
What is the main idea?
Where is Paula now?
Where does Paula live now?
What does Paula ask?
When did Paula buy the cake?
an expected action: it has already happened, or not yet
a situation from before: still going on, or over
a finished day: indefinido in every variety
how things used to be, different from now

Two questions, two pairs. Has the action happened? → ya / todavía no. Is the situation still true? → todavía / ya no. “Not yet” is todavía no, never “ya no”. And for the past: ayer + indefinido (a day), antes + imperfecto (another period).
—Have you finished the report yet? —No, not yet. I’ll finish it tomorrow.
My grandmother is ninety and still cooks every day, as when she was young.
Last night there was a storm and today the streets are wet.
I used to go to work by bus; now I go by bike.
Lucas has already had breakfast: he isn’t hungry.
A month later, Hugo starts a new job: he is now a teacher at a tourism school. Write his sentences with antes, ya no and todavía no.

An extra step, if you have time. Aún (with an accent) means the same as todavía. And in Mexico, in conversation, todavía no + present is very common for “not yet”: “Paula todavía no llega” = “Paula hasn’t arrived yet”.

Many adverbs are made with the feminine adjective + -mente: recientemente (recently), últimamente (lately), actualmente (currently, nowadays). If the adjective has a written accent, it keeps it: último → últimamente. Careful: actualmente does not mean “actually”; it means “now, these days”.
“Aún no llegó Paula” means…
A friend from Guadalajara says: “It’s nine and Rodrigo still hasn’t arrived”. What does it mean?
An email from the hotel: “The guest has not confirmed the booking yet”.
Hugo: “I used to work at a bank; these days I work at a school”.
The -mente adverb from “último” is…

You can now place things in time: “Ayer llegó Elena”, “Antes vivía cerca”, “Todavía no llegó nadie”. In class 054 you take the next step: you join two actions in one sentence with antes de, después de and cuando: “After dinner, I called Ana”. It is the natural next step: from antes on its own to antes de + an action.

Elena Ruiz coordinates the community garden on calle Sol. Tomorrow, Saturday, there is a planting day with the neighbours. Elena already has the list of jobs. Her phone rings: it’s Rosa, a neighbour. Elena tells her: “I’m going to call the neighbours early tomorrow”. Then, to Rosa, who is in a hurry: “OK, I’ll call you later”. Today you learn to choose between these two forms of the future.
I’m going to call the neighbours tomorrow. (a plan she already made)
I’ll call you later. (a promise she makes right now)
“Voy a llamar a los vecinos mañana” is…
“Te llamaré luego” is…
What are you going to do?
Tomorrow we’re going to plant tomatoes.
The neighbours are going to come at nine.
What will you do? What will happen?
I’ll call you later.
In July we’ll eat our own tomatoes.

Some verbs change their stem, with the same endings: tendré (I’ll have), podré (I’ll be able to), haré (I’ll do), saldré (I’ll leave), vendré (I’ll come), habrá (there will be). Today you only recognise them; you practise them in class 057.
On Saturday we’ll open the garden at nine.
Tomorrow I’ll be at the garden all morning.
Careful, Pablo! The glass is going to fall.
On Sunday temperatures will rise all over the country.
“What are you going to do on Saturday?” “I’m going to go to the garden.”
The garden will open on Saturday at nine.
Don’t worry, I’ll help you with the plants.

In everyday conversation in many Latin American countries, ir a + infinitive is much more frequent than the simple future. In Spain it is very frequent too. For a quick promise you also hear the present: “Vale, te llamo luego”. All three options are correct.

“Mañana”, “esta noche” or “luego” go with both forms: “Esta noche va a llover” (you see it coming) and “Esta noche te llamaré” (you promise it). What decides is what you want to do: tell a plan, point out a sign or make a promise.
A sign on the garden gate says: “The planting day will start at nine”.
“Pablo, what are you going to do tomorrow afternoon?” “I’m going to rest.”
This afternoon we’re going to water the lettuces.
I promise: tomorrow I’ll help you with the boxes.
Hi, Pablo! Thanks for coming. Tomorrow we’re going to plant the tomatoes and the lettuces.
Great! How many people are going to come?
About fifteen. The Ortiz family is going to bring the plants at nine. Everything is organised.
And the tools? There are only two spades here.
Yes, I know. I’m going to call Rosa right now: she has more.
Don’t worry. I have three at home: I’ll bring them tomorrow.
Thanks! Hey, look at those black clouds…
Oh, yes. It’s going to rain tonight.
Good: that way the soil will be soft for planting.
And when will we eat the first tomatoes?
In July, if all goes well. And one day we’ll sell vegetables at the neighbourhood market.
I’m sure we will! Well, I’m off. I’ll call you tonight to confirm the time.
Who is going to bring the plants?
What does Pablo promise?
Why does Pablo say “va a llover”?
On Saturday we’re going to plant the carrots.
Pablo: “Don’t worry, I’ll bring two big bottles of water”.
In August we’ll water the plants every day.
Careful, Mateo! You’re going to fall!
“One day the neighbourhood children will learn to grow vegetables here.”
Tomorrow we’re going to sow flowers.
I’ll call you after dinner.
The sky is very grey: it’s going to rain.
In September we’ll pick the pumpkins.
What is the main idea?
Why isn’t she going to arrive at nine?
What is Rosa going to bring?
Who is going to go with Rosa?
What does the radio forecast say?
a plan already made, or a sign you can see now
a promise, a distant prediction, a forecast or an announcement
the “a”, the infinitive and the accent

Ask yourself: is it already decided, or can you see it coming? → “Voy a llamar mañana”, “Va a llover”. Are you promising it now, imagining it far ahead or announcing it? → “Te llamaré luego”, “Algún día venderemos verduras”. Often both are possible; in conversation, ir a is the most frequent.
I’ve already booked the hotel: in June I’m going to travel to Lima.
“Will you help me with the move?” “Of course! I’ll help you on Saturday.”
The little boy is very sleepy: he’s going to fall asleep any minute.
I promise: we’ll finish the report tomorrow.
Airport announcement: “The flight from Bogotá will arrive twenty minutes late”.
A month later, Elena turns fifty. Pablo and Rosa prepare a surprise party at the garden. Write their sentences with the right form.
Elena writes to the volunteers’ chat with ir a. Now she writes the news item for the neighbourhood bulletin, a more formal text. There she uses the simple future.
What does “Habrá café para todos” mean?
What does “Los niños podrán regar las plantas” mean?

You can now choose between “voy a llamar” and “te llamaré”, and you know the regular forms of the simple future. In class 057 you work on the simple future in depth: the irregular forms (tendré, podré, haré, saldré, habrá…), promises and predictions. It is the natural next step: you already know when to use it; now you learn all its forms.

It is Saturday morning at the neighbourhood cultural centre. Rosa Medina runs a cooking workshop: today they are making a vegetable soup. Rosa uses tú with Pablo, her assistant, and usted with don Ernesto, a 72-year-old student. Valeria, a student from Córdoba (Argentina), uses vos. To give instructions, they all use the imperative.
Pablo, come here, please.
Pablo, come here, please. (Argentina)
Don Ernesto, come here, please.
Don Ernesto, come to this table.
Pablo, wash the vegetables.
“Vení” is…
Tú commands: take the tú present and drop the -s.
Cut the bread into slices.
Open the window, please.
Taste the broth before serving.
Vos commands: take the vos present and drop the -s. The stress stays at the end.
Cut the bread into slices. (vos)
Taste the broth before serving. (vos)
Turn on the heat.
Close the door, please. (vos)
Eight very common verbs have an irregular, short tú command. With vos, almost all of them are regular: the infinitive without the -r, with an accent (vení, poné).
“Sal un momento” is the verb salir (go out). “Pon sal en la sopa” is the noun (salt). Context decides.
Put the water in the big pot.
Tell the truth: do you like the soup?
Pablo, take a picture of the soup. (vos)
Usted commands: take the yo present, drop the -o and add the “other” vowel: -ar verbs take -e, -er/-ir verbs take -a.
Madam, cut the bread, please. (corto → corte)
Make the salad at this table. (hago → haga)
Go to the kitchen and ask for a plate. (ir → vaya · pido → pida)
This “other” vowel (corte, coma) is very important: in class 059 it comes back for negative tú commands: “no cortes”, “no comas”.
Set the table, please.
Eat a little more, don Ernesto.
Go to room two, please.

Voseo is normal in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, and in many parts of Central America. In some areas, for example parts of Colombia and Costa Rica, many people use usted with friends and family too. All three forms are correct.
In Spanish, the imperative is very normal for asking for things, especially with “por favor” and a friendly tone: “Pase, por favor”. It is not rude.
Come this way, please.
Come and eat, the soup is ready.
Be careful, the pot is hot.
Write your name on this list.
Good morning. Today we are making a vegetable soup. Pablo, come here and bring the carrots, please.
Here they are. What do I do now?
Wash the carrots and put water in the big pot.
Excuse me, Rosa. And what do I do?
Don Ernesto, come to this table. Here you are, here’s a knife. Cut the onion into small pieces.
Pablo, come here a moment. Taste the broth. Does it have enough salt?
Mmm… it needs a bit more, doesn’t it?
Yes. Bring the salt, please. It’s on your table.
Don Ernesto, now heat a little oil and put the onion in the pot.
All the onion? Now?
Yes, all of it. And Pablo, pop out for a moment and go and buy more tomatoes. Here, here’s some money.
On my way! I’ll be right back.
What does don Ernesto do first?
What does Valeria want?
Where does Pablo go at the end?
Put the clean plates in the cupboard, please.
Mrs Luisa, leave your coat here, please.
Pablo, close the window, it’s cold.
Don Ernesto, tell me the truth: is it good?
Pablo, go to the bakery and buy bread for everyone.
Come to the kitchen with me. (usted)
Put the salt and the oil on the table. (tú)
Make a shopping list for Saturday. (tú)
Try this tomato soup. (vos)
What is the main idea?
What does don Ernesto have to do first?
How long does the soup need?
What does he do at the end, if needed?
Why does he have to arrive early on Saturday?
tú present minus -s, plus eight short irregular forms
vos present minus -s, stress at the end, no vowel change
yo form minus -o, plus -e (-ar) or -a (-er/-ir)

First decide who you are talking to. With tú: the present without -s (corta, cierra) and eight short forms (ven, pon, haz…). With usted: start from “yo” and change the vowel (vengo → venga, corto → corte). With vos: the vos present without -s (vení, cortá).
A waiter to a customer: “Sir, take a seat here, please.”
To your sister: “Tell the truth: do you like my soup?”
To a friend: “Come early tomorrow: we leave at seven.”
At a hotel, to a guest: “Madam, go to the second floor, please.”
In Buenos Aires a friend says “Poné música”. How do you say it with tú?
Lucía works at a hotel reception. She explains the way to her colleague with tú; to a guest, with usted. Change her sentences to usted.

For ustedes, add -n to the usted form: venga → vengan, corte → corten, haga → hagan. In Latin America, ustedes works for everyone (friends or not). In most of Spain, with friends people use vosotros: the infinitive with -d (venid, cortad, haced).

You can now give instructions with tú and usted, and you understand vos: “ven”, “venga”, “vení”. Next comes saying what not to do. In class 059 the “other” vowel of usted (corte, coma) comes back: “no cortes”, “no comas”. It is the natural next step: you already know the form, now you use it to forbid and warn.

Nuria Campos is a graphic designer and lives in Mexico City with her friend Valeria. Yesterday she had a very important job interview, at half past nine. But the morning started badly: she woke up late and got nervous on the metro. Today you learn to tell a routine in the past and the changes in a person with me, te, se and nos.
“I woke up at ten past eight.”
“On the metro I got nervous.”
“Tonight I’m going to go to bed early.”
“Me desperté a las ocho y diez” is about…
“Me puse nerviosa” means…
In “voy a acostarme”, where is the pronoun?

You already know “me levanto, te duchas, se viste” (class 031) and the past tenses (classes 045–050). Today you put them together. The pronoun does not move when the tense changes: it goes before the conjugated verb. With the present perfect, it goes before he, has, ha.
Where does the pronoun go in the past?
Yesterday Nuria got up in a rush.
As a student, I used to get up at ten.
Today I woke up at six.
Last night Valeria went to bed at twelve.
Today I got up very early.
When she was a student, Nuria always got up at ten.
And with two verbs, or with an instruction?
I’m going to go to bed early.
I’m getting dressed.
Calm down, Nuria. Don’t worry.
Tomorrow I’m going to get up at six.
We have to go to bed early.
Valeria sees Nuria very nervous and says to her: “Calm down!”
What changed in the person?
On the metro, Nuria got nervous.
Valeria got worried because Nuria didn’t answer.
After the phone call, I calmed down.
At nine, Nuria was nervous.
Suddenly, Nuria got nervous.
When she saw the time, Nuria got very worried.
All morning Nuria was tired.
In the meeting, the clients got bored and looked at their phones.

“Te” is not always reflexive. “Te despiertas a las seis” = you wake up yourself. “Yo te despierto a las seis” = Valeria does the action and Nuria receives it. Look at the verb: if the verb’s person and the pronoun are the same person, it is reflexive.
Valeria woke Nuria up at six.
With the noise of the metro, Nuria got scared.
Nuria: “The night before I only slept five hours.”
Which one is correct?
I’m back! How was yesterday’s interview? You didn’t answer my messages and I got a bit worried.
Sorry, it was a crazy day! The night before I couldn’t sleep and I fell asleep at one. And the alarm didn’t go off.
No! And what time did you wake up?
At ten past eight, and the interview was at half past nine! I jumped out of bed, showered in five minutes and got dressed without having breakfast.
And did you get there on time?
Almost not. On the metro, the train stopped for ten minutes in a tunnel and I got really nervous.
Oh, poor you! And what did you do?
I called the studio and the receptionist calmed me down: “Don’t worry, we’ll wait for you.” I arrived at half past nine on the dot.
And the interview? How did it go?
At first I was nervous, but Mr Lozano was very nice and little by little I relaxed. Tomorrow I have the second interview, at eight!
Congratulations! So tonight don’t go to bed late, OK?
No, I’m going to go to bed at ten. And if the alarm doesn’t go off, will you wake me up at six?
Why did Nuria wake up late?
Who calmed Nuria down?
What is Nuria going to do tonight?
At the hotel, I woke up at half past six.
On the first day, my boss and her team went to bed very late.
For the presentation, the boss got dressed in a blue suit.
Before, at university, I always went to bed late.
I’m not working tomorrow, so I don’t have to get up early.
Nuria got nervous on the metro.
I’m going to go to bed early tonight.
I’m getting dressed for the interview.
Don’t worry about the alarm.
What is the main idea?
What happened to Iván in his first interview?
How did Iván calm down?
What advice does he give her for tonight?
What is Iván going to do tomorrow at half past six?

Reírse (to laugh) also takes a pronoun: me reí, se rio, nos reímos. Today “rio” is written without an accent. And notice “Yo te llamo”: Iván does the action and Nuria receives it, like “me dieron el trabajo” (they gave me the job).
in every tense; also before haber
infinitive, gerund, affirmative instruction; never in the middle
the moment when something changes in the person
someone else receives the action, or just a state

Ask first: does the action or the change stay in the same person? If yes, use me, te, se, nos: before the conjugated verb (me desperté, me he levantado) or attached to the infinitive, gerund or affirmative instruction (voy a acostarme, levántate). If someone else receives the action, or you only describe with estar, there is no se: despertó a Nuria, estaba nerviosa.
On Monday, Marina woke up late and missed the bus.
I can’t go out now: I’m having a shower.
When he saw the price, my father got a bit angry.
Tomorrow we have to get up at five.
Last night a very loud noise scared the children.
Marina, a friend of Nuria’s, started a new job in an office yesterday. Tell her first day with today’s rules.

Optional. At the interview, the receptionist and Mr Lozano speak to Nuria with usted. With usted, the pronoun is se: “No se preocupe”, “Siéntese” (sit down), “¿A qué hora se levanta usted?”. With ustedes too: “Siéntense”.
The receptionist, on the phone: “Don’t worry, we’ll wait for you.”
Mr Lozano: “Come in and sit down, please.”
Mr Lozano: “Do you get nervous when you speak in public?”
Mr Lozano to two candidates: “Please sit down here.”

You can now tell your routine in the past and the changes in a person: “me puse nerviosa”, “me tranquilicé”. In class 061 you look closely at two very common change verbs: ponerse (se puso triste, se puso roja) and quedarse (se quedó callada, se quedó sorprendido). It is the natural next step: you already know where the pronoun goes; now you learn which change each verb expresses.

On Saturday, Javier and his friend Elena threw a surprise party for Nuria: she was turning forty. When Nuria opened the door and saw all her friends, she went red and was left speechless. Later she saw her mother on a video call: she got sad and went quiet. In class 060 you used me, te, se… with routines and with changes like “se puso nervioso”. Today you learn two verbs to tell how a person changes: ponerse and quedarse.
Nuria got sad… (a quick change, a reaction)
…and went quiet. (the state she was left in)
“Nuria se puso roja” means…
“Nuria se quedó callada” means…
What happened to him or her at that moment?
Javier got nervous when the phone rang.
Nuria got very happy with the surprise.
I always go red when I speak in public.
When she saw her mother on the screen, Nuria got sad.
My sisters always get nervous before an exam.
How was he or she left afterwards?
Nuria was left speechless when she opened the door.
Uncle Ramiro fell asleep on the sofa.
With the news, we were all left surprised.
Where did he or she stay? Until when?
Marcos was ill and stayed at home.
Elena stayed at the party until three.
The film was very long and I fell asleep.
It was raining a lot and Elena stayed at home all Sunday.
At seven, Javier was calm. (a description)
At eight, Javier got nervous. (a quick change)
In the end, Javier was reassured. (the state he was left in)

Some words almost always go with one verb. With ponerse: nervous, red, happy, serious, ill. With quedarse: quiet, asleep, surprised, alone, speechless. Some go with both: “se puso triste” (the reaction) and “se quedó triste” (how she felt afterwards, for a while). In many Latin American countries people also say enfermarse: “me enfermé” = I got ill.
Today is Monday and Marcos is already well: he has no fever.
On Friday night, Marcos suddenly got ill.
With the bad news, everyone went quiet.
Javier put the cake on the table and turned off the light.
When she heard “Surprise!”, Nuria went very pale.
Elena, sorry about Saturday. On Friday night I got ill and stayed at home all weekend.
Don’t worry! Are you better now?
Yes, I’m fine now. But tell me: did the surprise work?
Almost not! At eight Nuria called: “I’ll be there in five minutes.” And Javier got nervous: the cake still wasn’t at home!
Poor Javier! And what did Nuria do when she opened the door?
We turned on the light and shouted “Surprise!”. She went red and was speechless for a minute.
No wonder! And then?
Then she got very happy and hugged us all. After that Javier called Nuria’s mother on a video call.
Rosa? She lives in Valencia, right?
Yes. When she saw her on the screen, Nuria got sad and went quiet. But Rosa sang “Happy Birthday” to her and Nuria smiled again.
How lovely! And how late did you stay?
I stayed until three. And uncle Ramiro fell asleep on the sofa at eleven, with the music really loud!
Why didn’t Marcos go to the party?
Why did Javier get nervous?
What happened to uncle Ramiro?
I always go red when I have to speak in front of a lot of people.
Lola, the neighbour, didn’t know anything. When she came in, she was left surprised.
At ten, Lola’s little boy fell asleep in her arms.
On Friday I got ill and didn’t go to the party.
It’s Sunday and Javier is very tired: he only wants to sleep.
Nuria went very red.
Yesterday I stayed at home.
The uncle fell asleep on the sofa.
When she saw her mother, she got sad.
What is the main idea?
How did Nuria react when she opened the door?
Why did she get a little sad?
What is Nuria doing today?
describes; there is no change
a quick change of mood, colour or health
the state the person is left in afterwards
not leaving, staying somewhere

Both verbs always take the pronoun: me puse, se quedó. Ponerse = the quick reaction (se puso roja). Quedarse = how the person is left afterwards (se quedó callada) or “to stay” (se quedó en casa). The adjective agrees: Nuria se puso roja, Javier se puso rojo. And the indefinido of poner is puso, never “ponió”.
My brother always goes red when he speaks in public.
Last night I watched a very long film and fell asleep on the sofa.
It was raining hard, so my girlfriend and I stayed at home.
When the doctor gave her the news, Ana went pale.
Pedro is ill now: he has a fever and won’t get out of bed.
Pablo, Elena’s brother, had a job interview yesterday. Tell his reactions with ponerse and quedarse.

Quedarse appears in very frequent expressions: quedarse sin + noun (I ran out of battery, money, cake), quedarse en blanco (my mind went blank) and quedarse dormido also meaning to oversleep. For bigger changes, of profession or character, at B1 and B2 you will see other verbs: “se hizo médica”, “se volvió muy tranquilo”, “se convirtió en un problema”. Today you only need to recognise them.
In the oral exam my mind went blank: I couldn’t remember anything.
My phone ran out of battery in the middle of the call.
This morning I overslept and got to work late.
Read: “Con los años, mi abuelo se volvió muy tranquilo.” What does it mean?

You can now tell how a person reacts: “se puso nerviosa”, “se quedó callada”, “me quedé en casa”. In class 062 you keep talking about how you feel, but with other verbs and other pronouns: “me duelen los pies” (my feet hurt), “me falta tiempo” (I’m short of time), “le interesa el arte” (he’s interested in art). It is the natural next step: now the pronoun says who something happens to, and the verb agrees with the thing that is liked, hurts or is missing.

Elena Duarte is a guide in Guanajuato, Mexico. Today she is with a small group: Rosa and Javier Medina, a married couple from Puebla, and Marcos Ibarra, a photographer. It is two in the afternoon and they walked all morning through streets with lots of steps. Javier sits down and says: “My feet hurt and I don’t have enough time for everything.” Today you learn the verbs that work like gustar.
I’m interested in museums.
My feet hurt.
I don’t have enough time.
What is wrong with Javier?
“Me falta tiempo” means…
In “me duelen los pies”, what hurts?
What are you interested in? What hurts? What do you lack?
Rosa is interested in Mexican art.
Javier’s right knee hurts.
We need two more hours to see everything.
Cars in narrow streets bother me.
Marcos is interested in street photography.
After so many steps, my legs hurt.
The heat bothers Javier.
To count the time left until a moment, faltar goes without me, te, le: “There are four hours left until the bus”, “It’s nearly six”. The same rule: four hours, plural; poco, singular.
Rosa is interested in getting to know the city’s museums.
We don’t have enough patience with so many tourists.
It’s ten minutes to six.
Yesterday my feet hurt a lot.
I’m interested in the museum; Javier isn’t. (contrast)
Javier’s knee hurts. (clarity: le can be him, her or you)
Rosa and Marcos love art.
The “a + person” part is optional; the pronoun is not. You say “A mí me gusta”, “A Javier le duele”, never “A mí gusta”. And “Mí me gusta” does not exist: always “a mí”.
Rosa and Javier love Guanajuato.
Elena to Javier (formal): “Does your knee hurt?”
I’m more interested in the market.
Elena to the group: “What are you all interested in?”
You will also hear hacer falta with the same pattern: “I need a map”, “We need two chairs”. It means “to need” and is common in Spain and Latin America.
Marcos: “I need a new battery for the camera.”
Javier: “My back hurts.”
Rosa: “This museum is very interesting.”
Which one is correct?
Which one is correct? (They are interested in visiting the mines.)
Right, it’s two o’clock and the bus to San Miguel leaves at six. What would you like to do this afternoon?
I’m interested in museums. There’s an art museum near here, isn’t there?
Yes, five minutes away. And you, Mr Medina?
I’m interested in the market, but I can’t do any more today: my feet hurt.
Of course, we climbed a lot of steps this morning. And your knee? Does it hurt too?
A little. And this sun really bothers me. I’d rather wait in the square, in the shade.
And you, Marcos? Aren’t you interested in the museum? It has a photography room.
Yes, very! But I also want to go up to the viewpoint: I still need the photos of the city from above.
There’s time for both. There are four hours left until the bus.
Thank goodness. I never have enough time when I travel.
So the two of you are interested in the museum, and Mr Medina rests in the square. See you here at quarter to six.
Great. And an ice cream for me, please!
Why doesn’t Javier go to the market?
What does Marcos still need?
How long is it until the bus?
Rosa loves the paintings in the big room.
Marcos is very interested in the old photo exhibition.
Are you interested in seeing the modern art room?
For my project, I still need ten photos.
I really liked the colonial art rooms.
Javier’s knee hurts.
We don’t have enough time for the market.
I’m interested in art museums.
Does the heat bother you (all)?
What is the main idea?
What was Marcos very interested in?
Why didn’t Javier go to the museum?
What didn’t they have enough time for?
What did Rosa buy for Paula?
one thing, something uncountable or an infinitive
several things, two things with “y”, a number
a + person is optional; the pronoun never is
-ó for one thing, -aron / -ieron for several

With gustar, interesar, doler, faltar and molestar, the verb looks at the thing: “Me falta tiempo”, “Me duelen los pies”. The person goes with me, te, le, nos, les, and to stress or clarify who, you add a + person: “A Javier le duelen los pies”. Never “yo duelo” or “a mí gusta”.
My sister is very interested in old films.
After the match, my legs hurt.
It’s five to nine: the class is about to start.
The street noise doesn’t bother my parents.
Last summer we really liked the village festivals.
A week later, Javier goes to the doctor in Puebla. The doctor reads her notes about Javier. You are Javier: say the same thing in your own words.

To react to what someone says: “A mí también” (me too), “A mí tampoco” (me neither), “A mí sí” (I do), “A mí no” (I don’t). And three more verbs with the same pattern: quedar (what you still have left: I have two days left), importar (¿le importa…? = would you mind…?) and preocupar (the weather worries me).
“I’m not interested in football.” “Me neither.”
“Javier doesn’t like the sun.” “Rosa does: she loves it.”
Quick! We only have ten minutes left before the bus.
Elena, on the bus: “Madam, would you mind closing the window?”
Because of Javier’s knee, Rosa is worried about the steps.

Today you used me, te, le, nos, les with verbs like gustar: “A Javier le duelen los pies”. In class 063 you use the same pronouns with verbs like give, send or say: “I sent the message to Lucía”. It is the natural next step: you can already choose between le and les and use a + person; now you use them to say who you give, send or tell something to.

Lucía has worked at the public library for six years. Now she is going back to Chile, and her colleagues are preparing a surprise party for Friday. Marta is organising everything. Yesterday she sent Lucía a message: “Are you free on Friday afternoon?”. Today you learn to say who you give, send, tell or ask something to.
Marta sent a message to Lucía.
Marta sent her a message.
Marta sent Lucía a message. (very common)
“Marta le mandó un mensaje.” What does “le” refer to?
Which sentence is correct and very natural?
To whom? Who receives something?
The director lent us the reading room.
Did Lucía answer you?
Rubén explained the plan to the colleagues.
“Mr Herrera, will you lend us the room?”
I wrote to all of them yesterday.
“Can you send me the address, please?”
Why “le” and also “a Lucía”?
I thanked Óscar.
I sent the colleagues the invitation yesterday.
I gave the present to her, not to her sister.
“She wrote to me, but not to you.” “A mí” is for contrast or emphasis, as in “a mí me gusta”. But “me” does not disappear: “A mí escribió” is wrong.
I told Óscar the time this morning.
We bought Lucía a photo album.
He gave the key to me.
I invited Lucía: I invited her.
I told Lucía the time: I told her the time.

In many parts of Spain people say “le vi” or “le invité” when the person is a man. This is called leísmo, and the RAE accepts it in that case (one man). With a woman or with things it is not accepted: “la vi”, “lo compré”. In this class we use lo / la, which is correct everywhere.
Marta called her on Monday with an excuse.
Marta asked Lucía: “Are you free on Friday?”.
I wrote to the afternoon colleagues yesterday.
I answered her straight away.
Marta, how is the party going? Have you sent the colleagues the invitation yet?
Yes, I wrote to everyone yesterday. And I sent Lucía a message: “Are you free on Friday afternoon?”.
And what did she answer you?
She said yes. She knows nothing. And Óscar? Did you invite him?
Yes, I saw him at the entrance and told him the time: at six, in the reading room.
Perfect! And the present? She loves photos.
I’ve already bought a beautiful album. Tomorrow I’ll ask everyone for a photo to put in it.
What a good idea! And is Mr Herrera lending us the room?
Yes, he gave me the key yesterday. On Friday we open at five.
Great. I’ll write the card to Lucía from all of us. Can you lend me your green pen?
Sure, here you are. And then you pass the card to me: I’ll keep it with the present.
What did Marta ask Lucía in her message?
Who told Óscar the time?
What is Rubén going to ask the colleagues for?
Marta asks Mr Herrera: “Can we use the blue chairs?”.
Rubén asks each colleague for a photo.
Marta sends them an email with the time.
“Marta, can you send me the exact address of the room?”
“Yes, I’ll send you a message with everything now.”
I asked the colleagues for a photo.
They gave the key to me.
The director lent us the room.
Óscar brought Lucía flowers.
What is the main idea?
How did Marta prepare the surprise?
Who did Lucía send photos of the album to?
Why did she leave Mr Herrera a note?
What is Lucía going to send them tomorrow?
the person who receives something; same for a man, a woman and usted
I, you, we, you all (Spain): the same forms as with gustar
very common; needed with the person first and with a mí, a él, a ella, a usted
the person who is seen, called, invited: lo / la; the person who receives: le

Ask: to whom? If the person receives something (a message, the time, a present), use me, te, le, nos, os, les before the verb: “Le mandé el mensaje”. One person: le; several: les. You can also name the person: “Le mandé el mensaje a Lucía”, and if the person comes first, “le” is needed: “A Lucía le mandé el mensaje”.
Tomorrow is my sister’s birthday: I’m going to give her a book.
My parents live far away, so I write to them every Sunday.
I saw your sister at the market and said hello to her.
Can you explain this exercise to me? I don’t understand it.
They never tell us anything.
A month later, a new colleague arrives at the library: Nuria. Everyone helps her on her first day. Write the sentences with the pronoun.
For fast learners or if there is time left: a formal email, leísmo in Spain and “a mí” for contrast.
Mrs Paredes: I am writing to invite you to Lucía’s farewell party.
In Madrid, Rubén says “A Óscar le vi en la entrada”. What about this sentence?
We thanked the colleagues and invited them to another party.
Lucía wrote to all of us, but she wrote to me twice.

You can now say who you give or send something to: “Le mandé el mensaje a Lucía”. But what if you also want to replace “el mensaje” with a pronoun? Then there are two pronouns together, and “le” changes: “Se lo mandé”. In class 064 you learn to combine them: me lo, te la, se lo. It is the natural next step: you already know lo / la, and now le / les too.

Rosa Medina is retiring after thirty years at a travel agency. Today is her farewell party, and it is a surprise. Her colleagues give her a photo album. In the afternoon, Lorena asks: “Hugo, did you give Rosa the album?” And Hugo answers: “Yes, I gave it to her.” Today you learn to use two pronouns together: one for the person and one for the thing.
Hugo gave the album to Rosa.
Hugo gave it to her.
In “Hugo se lo dio”, what is “lo”?
In “Hugo se lo dio”, what is “se”?
—Did you give Rosa the album? —Yes, I gave it to her.
To whom? What?
The card? Lorena gave it to me this morning.
Your recipe book? I’ll give it back to you on Thursday.
The party photos? Hugo sent them to us last night.

With a conjugated verb (di, doy, mandó, prestas), both pronouns go together and in front: “Se lo di”, “¿Me la prestas?”. “No” goes before both: “No se lo di”. With an infinitive (“voy a dárselo”, I’m going to give it to him) or an imperative (“dámelo”, give it to me) the position changes: you will see that in class 065.
Your camera? I’ll give it back to you tomorrow.
The photos? Hugo sent them to us too.
What happens to le and les?
I gave Rosa the book. → I gave it to her.
I sent my colleagues the photos. → I sent them to them.
The surprise? Nobody told Rosa about it.

“Se” can be many people. If the context does not make it clear, add the person at the end: “Se lo di a Rosa”, “Se lo di a ellos”, “Se lo doy a usted”. This repetition is normal and correct in Spanish.
I lent Hugo my umbrella. → I lent it to him.
I showed the clients the office. → I showed it to them.
I gave Rosa the flowers. → I gave them to her.
I gave my children the album. → I gave it to them.

Look only at the thing: the album → lo, the card → la, the books → los, the flowers → las. Rosa is a woman, but “¿El álbum? Se lo di”. And if the thing comes at the start of the sentence, the pronoun repeats it: “La tarjeta la tengo yo” (I’ve got the card), “El álbum se lo dio Hugo” (Hugo gave her the album).
The cake? Lorena took it to Rosa at the table.
I sent the invitation to everyone. → I sent it to them.
The travel books? Pilar gave them to Rosa.
The office keys? Yesterday I gave them to Pilar.
—Did you tell Rosa the time of the party? —No, I didn’t tell her.
Hugo, the party is at five. Shall we go through the list? First, the photo album.
Haven’t you got it?
No, Pilar asked me for it yesterday. She wants to write a few words on the first page.
Good. And the card with the signatures?
The whole office has signed it. I’ll give it to you now and you give it to Rosa at the party.
Perfect. And the travel books?
I bought them on Monday, but I haven’t shown them to Pilar yet.
Don’t worry, I’ll show them to her this afternoon. And the flowers?
The florist is bringing them to us at four. Hey, Rosa doesn’t know anything, right?
No, nobody told her. Well… yesterday her daughter asked me the time of the party and I told her.
Hugo! Well, her daughter can keep a secret. But you don’t tell Rosa, OK?
Why hasn’t Lorena got the album?
Who gives Rosa the card at the party?
What did Hugo tell Rosa’s daughter?
The bouquet? Pilar gave it to Rosa with a hug.
The photos? Hugo is sending them to everyone tonight.
Your new number? Will you write it down for me here, in my diary?
Your camera? Yes, I’ll give it back to you tomorrow.
The travel books? Hugo gave them to Rosa after the cake.
I gave it to Rosa yesterday.
Will you lend it to me tomorrow?
I haven’t sent them to him yet.
Rosa is giving it back to you on Thursday.
What is the main idea?
Who told Rosa that the party was Lorena’s idea?
Who did Rosa show the album to last night?
How did the flowers get to Rosa’s house?
What does Rosa have that belongs to Lorena?
first to whom, then what; together, before the verb
“se” = to him, to her, to you (usted), to them
lo, la, los, las agree with the thing, not the person

Two pronouns together: first the person, then the thing, both before the conjugated verb: “Te la doy”, “No se lo dije”. Le and les become se before lo, la, los, las. And the second word looks only at the thing: “¿El álbum? Se lo di a Rosa”.
The umbrella? My neighbour lent it to me yesterday.
The car keys? I’ve already given them to your brother.
I told my parents the news. → I told them.
Ana’s email? I’ll forward it to you right now.
—Who explained the exercise to you? —The teacher explained it to us.
A month later, Rosa has time for her neighbours and her family. Replace the words with two pronouns.
“Se” is also usted and ustedes, so you hear it a lot in shops and offices. And in many parts of Latin America you will hear a very common colloquial form: “Ya se los dije”.
Is the book a present? Shall I wrap it for you?
Which sentence is clearer?
What does “se los dije” mean here?

In general usage, “lo” goes with the thing: “Ya se lo dije (a ustedes)”. In colloquial speech in many parts of Latin America, “Ya se los dije” is very common to show that the person is plural. Understand it when you hear it; in your exercises, use the general rule.

You can now use two pronouns before a conjugated verb: “Se lo di”, “Te la doy”. In class 065 you see what happens with an infinitive and with the imperative: “Voy a dárselo” or “Se lo voy a dar”, “Dámelo”. It is the natural next step: you already know the pairs (me lo, se la…); now you learn where they go when the verb is not conjugated or when you give an instruction.

Irene Salas is leaving tomorrow on a one-week work trip. Her neighbour, Mateo Ruiz, is going to look after her apartment: the plants, Nube the cat and the post. Tonight Irene gives him instructions. Today you learn where the pronoun goes with the imperative, the infinitive and the gerund.
Water them every two days.
Don’t water them too much.
You have to water them (both orders are correct).
In “Riégalas”, the pronoun “las” goes…
Irene doesn’t want much water on the plants. She says: “Don’t water them too much.”
Where does it go with a conjugated verb and with “no”?
Mateo waters them on Mondays.
Don’t open it at night.
Don’t call me before nine.
Where does it go with an affirmative command and with a lone infinitive?
Call me tonight.
Close it before you go out.
I need a glass to water them.
The window: “Close it before you go out, please.”
The letters: “Mateo looks for them in the mailbox every afternoon.”
I use a small glass to water them.
And with two verbs together?
I’m going to call you tomorrow.
Can I open it?
I’m looking for it.
