Which sentence is correct?
“Voy a verla” means the same as…
Mateo is making dinner right now: “I’m making it.”

Attach the pronoun and count the syllables from the end. If the stressed syllable is the third or fourth from the end, write an accent: llámame, escríbeme, haciéndolo. If it is the second, no accent: verla, comprarlo, dime.
The door: which one is spelled correctly? (Close it.)
I want to see her before the trip.
I’m eating it now.

In Spain, vosotros is used for several people you know well. Before “os” the final -d drops: sentaos (sit down), levantaos. Exception: idos (go away). With other pronouns the -d stays: decídmelo, hacedlo. In Latin America ustedes is used: siéntense, váyanse. You only need to recognise these.
With vos the stress of the command falls on another syllable: comprá → compralo, no accent mark. With tú: cómpralo. Both are correct, each in its own variety.
Do you know where my charger is? Tell me, please!
Tomorrow’s exercise: do it today.
With usted, to the lady on the third floor: “The keys, put them here, please.”
Nube’s photos: “I’m going to send them to you tonight.”
The parcel: “Don’t open it yet, it’s a surprise.”
Thanks for coming, Mateo. Look, these are the keys to the apartment. Keep them safe, okay?
Sure, I’m going to put them with mine. What do I do with the plants?
Water them every two days, but don’t water them too much: just one glass of water.
Okay. And the cat? What does Nube eat?
Her food is in the kitchen cupboard. Give her a little in the morning and a little at night.
And the balcony window? Can I open it to let some air in?
Yes, but don’t leave it open: Nube loves going out onto the balcony.
Got it. Hey, what are you looking for?
My phone charger. I’ve been looking for it for ten minutes.
Here it is, on the sofa! Take it.
Thanks! And if there’s any problem, call me or text me. Don’t send me emails: I don’t read them when I travel.
Don’t worry. I’m going to send you a photo of Nube every day.
How does Mateo have to water the plants?
Why shouldn’t he leave the balcony window open?
How does Irene want to get news?
Nube, your food is here. Eat it!
The balcony door makes a noise. Can I fix it tomorrow?
Yes, thanks. But don’t fix it with cooking oil.
Irene, where is the new bag? I’m looking for it and I can’t find it.
It’s in the top cupboard. Open it and call me if it isn’t there.
I’m going to call you tonight.
Don’t water them today.
I have to take it out today. (the rubbish)
I’m giving it to her now. (the food, to Nube)
What is the main idea?
Where can Mateo pick up the parcel?
What happens if Mateo can’t pick it up?
What does Mateo have to do about the mailbox key?
with “no” and with a single conjugated verb
affirmative commands and a lone infinitive; watch the accent mark
before the first verb or attached at the end; never in the middle

Affirmative command: attached (riégalas, dímelo). With “no”: before (no las riegues). With two verbs: either position (las voy a regar = voy a regarlas). And the accent: if the word grows and the stress ends up third from the end, write it (cómpralo, haciéndolo); dime, hazlo and comprarlo don’t need one.
The keys are on the table. “Take them before you go out.”
The cake is for dinner. “Don’t eat it yet, please.”
Can you help me with the suitcase? — Yes, I can help you after lunch.
And dinner? — I’m making it. It’s almost ready.
The book: “Put it here, on the table.”
A month later, Mateo goes away and now Irene looks after his dog, Rulo. Mateo leaves her instructions. Replace the noun with a pronoun.
To go further: the same system with usted and ustedes, two pronouns with a periphrasis, and the expression “hay que”.
Irene to Mrs Lidia, the older neighbour: “My letters, please give them to Mateo.”
To Mrs Lidia: “The street door, please don’t leave it open.”
Mateo to two neighbours: “The meeting is here. Sit down, please.”
Irene’s keys: “I’m going to give them to you on Sunday.”
“The plants need watering” with a pronoun:

You can now put pronouns in the right place: “Riégalas”, “No las riegues”, “Las voy a regar”. In class 066 you learn another way to avoid repeating words: joining two sentences with “que”. It is the natural next step: after replacing nouns with pronouns, you learn to describe people and things inside the same sentence.

Rocío Medina has lived in a new building, on the third floor, since Sunday. On Monday a parcel arrived for her, but Rocío was at work. The delivery man left it with a neighbour. Today Rocío knocks on a door on the second floor and says: “Hi, I’m looking for the woman who lives here.” Today you learn to join a noun and a piece of information with “que”.
I’m looking for a woman. The woman lives here.
I’m looking for the woman who lives here.
In “Busco a la mujer que vive aquí”, who lives here?
What is “que vive aquí” for?
Which person? Which thing? Which place?
Rocío is the neighbour who arrived on Sunday.
The lift on the right isn’t working.
Do you know the café that opened in the square?
I use the door that opens onto the street.
The windows that face the park are big.
In “la tienda que está en la esquina”, the antecedent is…
The neighbour who picked up the parcel is Elena.
The parcel I bought is a present.
“Que” already stands for the noun, so you don’t repeat it with a pronoun: “el paquete que compré”, not “el paquete que lo compré”.
The chair I have in the living room is my grandmother’s.
In “la carta que escribió Elena”, who wrote?
The man who repairs the lift is very kind.
It’s the parcel that arrived on Monday.
Which parcel are you looking for?
The box (that) I bought is big.
In this kind of sentence (noun + information, no commas) use “que”, also for people: “la mujer que vive aquí”, not “la mujer quien vive aquí”. “Quien” has other uses you will see later, in class 100.
Which neighbour picked up your parcel?
The neighbour who picked up my parcel is called Elena.
“The box I bought is big”, in Spanish:
Which sentence is correct? (The photos I took are nice.)
The girls who live on the fifth floor study medicine.
Hi, Amparo. I’m looking for the parcel that arrived for me yesterday. It’s a present for my mother.
Oh, yes. The delivery man who came yesterday didn’t find you at home.
Of course, yesterday I worked until eight. So where did he leave it?
He gave it to the neighbour who lives in 2A. She works from home on Mondays.
Is she the woman who has a red bike?
No, that’s Marta, from the fourth floor. Elena is the young woman you met in the lift on Monday.
Oh, Elena! Very nice. I’ll go up now, then.
Wait, take the note the delivery man left. It has your name and the parcel number.
(At 2A) Hello, good afternoon. I’m looking for the woman who lives here. Is Elena in?
Hi. No, she’ll be back at nine. Are you the neighbour who’s expecting a parcel?
Yes, that’s me. Rocío, from 3B.
Elena told me about you, but I don’t know where the box she put away is. She’ll send you a message tonight.
Why doesn’t Rocío have her parcel?
Who is Elena?
What does Amparo give Rocío?
Who is the man with such a big dog?
The letters that arrived today are in your mailbox.
The lamp I bought is from a shop in my neighbourhood.
The students who live on the fourth floor are very nice.
Which key opens the garage?
I’m looking for the neighbour who lives on the second floor.
The parcel that arrived yesterday is for Rocío.
The flowers Hugo bought are lovely.
Do you know the man who has a big dog?
What is the main idea?
What is the box like?
When can Rocío come by?
What does the delivery man do if you are not at home?
Who is Hugo?
the noun does the action; the verb agrees with it
someone else does the action; don’t repeat the noun
que never disappears and has no accent

A noun + que + information to say which one: “la vecina que vive en el segundo”, “el paquete que compré”. Que works for people, things and places, never changes, has no accent and never disappears. If someone else does the action, don’t add lo or la.
The train that leaves at eight arrives in Valencia at eleven.
Do you like the jacket I bought myself?
The students who arrive late wait outside.
Which book are you reading?
Ana is the classmate I met on the English course.
A month later, Rocío starts a new job. She writes to Elena about her first day. Join the sentences with “que”.

To go further: when we already know what we are talking about, we don’t repeat the noun. “Which key is it? — The one with the red ribbon.” The article agrees with the noun you leave out: el que, la que, los que, las que.
Which key is the garage one? — The one with the red ribbon.
Which neighbours make noise? — The ones who live on the fifth floor.
There are two boxes. The big one is Elena’s and the one I bought is the small one.
Which man is Hugo? — The one with the dog.
Which sentence is about a specific person Rocío already knows?

You can now identify people and things with “que”: “la vecina que vive en el segundo”, “el paquete que compré”. In class 067 you give information about places and moments with donde and cuando (“the place where we met”), and talk about ideas with no noun using lo que (“what I need is a rest”). It is the natural next step: the same mechanism, with more kinds of antecedent.

On Saturday it will be ten years since Elena and Raúl got together. Their friend Nuria is a photographer and is going to take photos in the important places of their story for an album. Elena looks at an old photo and says: “This is the place where we met.” Today you learn to join two ideas in one sentence to talk about a place, a time or a thing without repeating words.
This is the café where we met.
In 2016, when I was a student, Raúl worked here.
What I like most is this photo.
Where did Elena and Raúl meet?
In this sentence, “lo que” means…
What happens in that place?
We met in the café. → It’s the café where we met.
It’s the street where we lived for three years.
It’s the café where Raúl used to work.
This is the square where Elena used to read on Sundays.
It’s the flat where we lived for three years.
What was going on at that time?
In 2016, when Elena was at university, she met Raúl.
On Sundays, when it’s sunny, we go to the park.
I remember the day we met very well.
It was the year I started working.

In English you say “the day when we met”. In Spanish, after el día, el año or el momento, the normal choice is que or en que: “el día que nos conocimos”, “el año en que nací”. Cuando fits better after a date or a period, with a comma: “En 2016, cuando yo estudiaba…”.
In 2019, when we lived on Luna Street, we bought our first sofa.
Which sentence sounds most natural?
Which thing? (without naming it)
What I like most about this photo is your smile.
This is what we need: time for ourselves.
Nuria always does what she promises.
What do you want for the album?
What I want is a simple album.
What I like most about the flat is the terrace.
What do you want to do on Saturday?
It’s the café that opened in 2010.
It’s the café where we met.
It’s the house that my parents bought.
It’s the house where my father was born.
I don’t understand what is happening with the camera.
It’s the bar where Raúl worked as a waiter.
What I need now is a coffee.
Look at this photo: it’s the café where we met.
So young! It was in 2016, when I was at university and you worked there as a waiter.
Yes. And this is the table where you always sat, next to the window.
And you always brought me a coffee that I hadn’t ordered!
Well… it was an excuse to talk to you.
And this one? It’s Luna Street, isn’t it? The flat where we lived for three years.
Yes. It was very small, but what I liked most was the terrace.
Do you remember the day we arrived with all the boxes? It was pouring with rain.
And the lift wasn’t working! Well, for the album, do you want something serious, in a studio?
No, what I want is something natural: photos without poses.
Perfect. So, for Nuria: the café, Luna Street and the bridge where I asked you to marry me.
And the park by the river, where we spent our Sundays, when we didn’t have money for anything else!
What was Raúl doing in 2016?
What did Raúl like most about the flat on Luna Street?
What does Elena want for the album?
On Saturday we start at the café where Elena and Raúl met.
I have a new camera that takes very good photos in low light.
The terrace was what Raúl liked most about the flat.
This is the bookshop where I worked for two summers.
In 2018, when we lived on Luna Street, we adopted a cat.
What I like most is the terrace.
This is the street where we live.
In 2016, when I was at university, I met Raúl.
What is the main idea?
What did Elena and Raúl do in the park by the river?
When did Raúl propose to Elena?
Why does Raúl want to start at nine?
What does Elena like most?
what happens in that place: the sentence needs “en”
cuando after a date or period; with día or año, que
what, the thing that: always “lo”
the noun does the action or receives it

Test it with two sentences: “Nos conocimos en el café” → “el café donde nos conocimos”. If there is no en (“Alquilamos el piso”), use que: “el piso que alquilamos”. If there is no noun before, use lo que: “Lo que quiero es descansar”. And for time: “En 2016, cuando…”, but “el día que…”.
This is the school where I studied as a girl.
What worries me is the weather: they say it’s going to rain.
It’s a city that has a lot of museums.
In August, when it’s very hot, the city is empty.
The bars where we used to meet our friends don’t exist any more.
After the shoot, Nuria shows her studio to a new client. Join the sentences as Nuria would.

An extra step, if you have time. “Donde” can take other prepositions: de donde (from where: venir de), por donde (through where: pasar por). And “lo que” appears in very common expressions: todo lo que (everything that) and lo que pasa es que… (the thing is…), useful to explain a problem.
Valparaíso is the city Nuria comes from.
This is the path we go along every morning.
Thank you for everything you did for us.
Elena: “Sorry, Nuria. The thing is, I’m working late today.” What is Elena doing?

You can now describe places, times and ideas precisely: “el café donde nos conocimos”, “en 2016, cuando…”, “lo que más me gusta…”. In class 068 you take the next step: you compare those places and things with mejor, peor, mayor and menor: “Este café es mejor que el otro”. It is the natural next step: first you describe, then you compare.

Sofía Rivas is a guide in Puerto Alba, a small city by the sea. Today she is showing the old town to two visitors, Irene and Marcos. In the square there is a fifty-metre tower. Sofía says: “It is the tallest building in the city”. And Irene answers: “It is really, really tall!”. Today you learn to say that something is number one in a group, and that something is very, very tall, good or pretty.
The tower is taller than the church. (two things)
The tower is the tallest building in the city. (number one in a group)
The tower is really, really tall. (no comparison)
“The tower is the tallest building in the city” means…
“La torre es altísima” means…
Which one is number one in a group?
Calle del Agua is the narrowest street in the old town.
These are the quietest neighbourhoods in the city.
Playa Norte is the least known beach on the coast.
The San Juan market is the oldest market in the city.
It is the biggest square in the old town.
Which one is the best? Who is the oldest?
This is the best coffee in the neighbourhood.
At two o’clock it is boiling hot: it is the worst time of day to climb the tower.
Marcos is sixty-two: he is the oldest in the group.
For Sofía, Casa Lola is the best restaurant in the port.
Irene is twenty-five and her sisters are thirty and thirty-two. Irene is the youngest of the three.
Is it very, very tall? Very, very good?
The empanadas are really, really good.
The way to the port is super easy.
Today there are loads of people in the square.
Calle del Agua is very, very long.
The mango juice is delicious.
How do I react when something impresses me?
How tall! (the tower)
What a beautiful view!
This coffee is so good!
Irene sees the beach from the tower. She says: “What a beautiful beach!”
Sofía compares two cafés: “The café on the square is cheaper than the one at the port”.
This is the worst hotel in the city.
The soup is really, really good.
This is the Clock Tower. It is fifty metres tall: it is the tallest building in the city.
How tall! Can you go up?
Yes, but there are a hundred and twenty steps. It is the hardest part of the walk.
No problem. I am the oldest in the group, but I am fit.
(At the top) What a beautiful view! You can see the whole port from here.
For me, it is the best place in Puerto Alba to take photos.
And that very narrow street, next to the church?
It is Calle del Agua, the narrowest in the old town. It is only one metre wide.
I’m hungry. Where can we eat something typical?
At the café on the square. The cheese empanadas are really good and really cheap.
Perfect. Yesterday I had the worst coffee of the trip: it was awful.
Not here, I promise. It is the least touristy café on the square, and the tastiest.
What is special about the Clock Tower?
Who is the oldest in the group?
Why does Sofía recommend the café on the square?
Calle del Agua is the narrowest street in Puerto Alba.
The San Juan market is the oldest in the city.
The empanadas on the square are the best in the city.
Marcos is the oldest in the group.
Try the flan! It is really, really good.
It is the tallest building in the city.
The empanadas here are really good.
Irene is the youngest of three sisters.
What is the main idea?
Where and when do they meet tomorrow?
What is special about the San Juan market?
Why are they going up the hill?
What does Sofía say about Casa Lola?
Why do they need to bring water and a cap?
number one in a group; the group goes with de
no “más”; mejor and peor go before the noun
very, very: no comparison and no “muy”
a strong reaction; qué with an accent

Ask yourself: two things, a group, or no comparison? Two things: “más alta que la iglesia”. A group: “el edificio más alto de la ciudad”, “el mejor café del barrio”. No comparison: “altísima”, “¡Qué alta!”. And never say it twice: not “el más mejor” and not “muy buenísimo”.
April is the best month to visit the coast: it is not hot and it does not rain.
August is the hottest month of the year.
Thanks for the present! It is really lovely.
It is the biggest lake in the country.
Your friends show you photos of their trip. You say: “What lovely photos!”
Clara lives in another city and writes notes for Sofía’s website. Her notes are correct, but a bit flat. Transform each note with the structure you are asked for.

Two very common structures. First: “uno de los / una de las” + plural noun + más + adjective + de: “It is one of the most beautiful cities on the coast” (not number one, but in the top group). Second: superlative + que + present perfect, for your own experience: “It is the best coffee I have ever had”.

In Mexico and other parts of Latin America, “bien” + adjective often means “very”: “La sopa está bien rica”. In informal speech in many countries you also hear “súper”: “súper barato”. These are colloquial; -ísimo works everywhere. And with the perfect: in many parts of Latin America people also say “el mejor café que probé” (class 051).
Puerto Alba is one of the most beautiful cities on the coast.
It is the best sea bream I have ever eaten.

You can now say what is number one in a group (“el edificio más alto de la ciudad”, “el mejor café del barrio”) and react strongly (“¡Qué alta!”, “buenísimo”). In class 070 you learn to talk about things and people without naming them: “Is there anything typical to eat?”, “There is nobody in the tower”. It is the natural next step: after quantity and degree, you talk about existence: something or nothing, someone or no one.

Marta Salcedo is a photographer. This week she is working in Oaxaca, in Mexico, and staying at the Casa Jacaranda hotel. In the evening she comes back and asks at the front desk: “Did anyone call me? Is there anything for me?”. Inés, the receptionist, answers: “Nobody called, but someone left something for you”. Today you learn four very useful words: algo, nada, alguien and nadie.
Someone left something for you. (a person and a thing, not named)
Nobody called. The box doesn’t say anything. (zero people, zero things)
In “Alguien dejó algo”, “alguien” is…
“No llamó nadie” means…
“The box doesn’t say anything”: what is written on it?
Is there a thing? Is there a person? (we don’t say which one)
Someone is at the door.
Marta wants to eat something before going to bed.
There’s something in the box: some photos.
How many things? How many people? Zero.
Nobody knows who left the box.
Marta has nothing in the fridge in her room.
—Who is at the front desk? —Nobody.
Someone is knocking at Marta’s door.
“I don’t know who left the box. Nobody saw it.”
Marta opens the box: there’s something inside, some photos.

In English, anything and anybody work in questions and in negative sentences. In Spanish they are two different words. In an ordinary question: algo / alguien (“Do you want anything?”, “Does anybody know…?”). In a negative sentence: nada / nadie (“I don’t want anything”, “Nobody knows”).
“Good evening. Do you need anything?”
—Did anybody ask for me? —No, nobody.
—Is there anything in the mailbox? —No, there’s nothing.
Nobody came. Nothing happened. (after the verb: put no before the verb)
Nobody came. Nobody answered. (first in the sentence: no “no”)

“No vino nadie” and “Nadie vino” mean the same. In conversation, “No vino nadie” is very common. What doesn’t work is “Nadie no vino” (extra no) or “Vino nadie” (missing no). In class 072 you practise more with nunca and other negative words.
Nobody called for Marta this afternoon.
This afternoon nobody called for Marta.
Nothing happened at the hotel today: a quiet day.

In Spanish, when a person receives the action, we put a before them: “I see Inés”, “I’m waiting for my colleague”. Alguien and nadie work the same way, because they are people: “I see someone”, “I don’t know anybody”. After hay there is no a: “There’s someone at the door”.
Marta doesn’t know anybody in Oaxaca.
There’s someone on the terrace.
Inés sees someone with a camera in the street.
—Would you like anything from the kitchen? —No, thanks, I don’t want anything.
Raúl: “Last night nobody came into the hotel after midnight.”
Good evening, Ms Salcedo. Do you need anything?
Good evening, Inés. Yes, a question: did anyone call me this afternoon? I’m expecting a call from my colleague Óscar.
I’m sorry. Nobody called for you today.
How strange. And did anything arrive for me? I’m expecting a small parcel.
Yes, someone left this box for you.
Great! Who left it?
I don’t know. I didn’t see anybody: when I came back from lunch, the box was already here, on the counter.
And the box doesn’t say anything? Doesn’t it have a name?
Nothing. It only says “Room 12”. Tomorrow I’ll ask someone in the kitchen.
Oh, look! There’s a note inside: “I came by the hotel, but I didn’t find anybody at the front desk. I’m leaving you the photos. Óscar”.
Oops, that’s true! At that time there was nobody here. I’m sorry.
Don’t worry about it. I have the photos now, and that’s what matters.
Who called Marta this afternoon?
Why doesn’t Inés know who left the box?
What is inside the box?
Waiter: “Good morning. Would you like anything to drink? Coffee, juice?”
Does anybody know what time the market opens?
Raúl: “Nobody called for you last night.”
She looks on the table in her room, but there’s nothing there.
Someone left a newspaper on Marta’s table.
Nobody called for you.
Someone left something at the front desk.
Is there anyone on the terrace?
What is the main idea?
Who saw the man with the box?
What did that man do?
Who called for Marta today?
Did they find the charger?
in yes sentences and ordinary questions (any- in questions)
after the verb, with no; at the start, without no
with hay and with things, no a

Two questions: thing or person? (algo / nada, alguien / nadie) and yes or no? In an ordinary question, any- is algo / alguien. If nada or nadie come after the verb, put no before it: “No vino nadie”. If nadie comes first, no “no”: “Nadie vino”. And with people who receive the action: a alguien, a nadie.
—Is there anyone in the meeting room? —No, it’s empty.
My brother was ill and didn’t eat anything all day.
It’s my first day at the company and I don’t know anybody.
I rang the bell three times, but nobody opened the door.
Listen: someone is singing upstairs.
A week later, Óscar is back at his office in Mexico City. His boss asks him questions. Óscar says no to everything: write his full answers.

An extra step, if you have time. These words appear in many useful phrases: algo / nada + a masculine adjective (“something tasty”, “nothing new”), algo de + infinitive (“something to eat”, “something to drink”), and más after them: “Anything else? — Nothing else, thanks”, “Anyone else? — Nobody else”.
With a verb like gustar, nada can mean “not at all”: “I didn’t like the film at all”. You only need to understand it; in class 072 you see more negative sentences like this one.
In a shop: “Here are your tortillas. Anything else?” — “Nothing else, thanks.”
Marta is hungry: “Is there anything to eat in the kitchen?”
—How was the meeting? —Same as always. They didn’t say anything new.
“No me gustó nada el hotel” means…
Inés: “I already have two volunteers for the trip. Does anyone else want to come?”

You can now talk about things and people without saying which: “Someone left something”, “Nobody came”. In class 071 you take the next step: words that go with a noun and say how many: “Is there any table free?”, “There’s no table left”, “There are a lot of people”. It is the natural next step: from alguien and nadie on their own to alguno and ninguno with a noun.

Lucía Herrera works at an architecture office. Her colleague Pilar is moving to another city, and Lucía is organising a farewell dinner for sixteen people. She calls the restaurant El Patio. The manager, Ramiro, answers: “Sorry, there isn’t a single free table left on the terrace on Saturday. But we have some big tables in the dining room.” Today you learn to say whether something exists or not (alguna, ninguna) and how much there is (mucho, poco, demasiado).
Do you have a free table? (any table at all)
There isn’t a single free table left.
There are a lot of tables in the dining room.
“No queda ninguna mesa libre” means…
Do you have a table for sixteen people?
There are a lot of big tables in the dining room.
Does it exist? Is there one, or a few?
Is there a good restaurant near the office?
Some colleagues are coming by car.
I have no problem with Saturday.

If “ninguno” comes after the verb, you put “no” before the verb: “No queda ninguna mesa”. If it comes before the verb, there is no “no”: “Ninguna mesa está libre”. In class 072 you work on this double negative with nadie, nada and nunca.
There’s no problem, madam.
Do you have high chairs? Yes, we have some.
Is there any space left on the terrace? No, there’s none left.
How much is there? How many are there?
A lot of people want to come to the dinner.
There isn’t much light in the dining room.
There’s too much noise on the terrace.
How much does someone work, eat or talk?
Pilar works a lot.
My colleagues don’t sleep much before a deadline.
In meetings, they talk too much.
Lucía and Nuria work a lot.
There aren’t many tables for a big group on the terrace.
There’s too much noise in the street: we can’t talk.
The dining room is very nice.
I like it a lot.
There’s a lot of space.

Before mejor, peor, mayor, menor, más and menos you use mucho, not muy: “El salón es mucho mejor para un grupo”, “Es mucho más barato”. And remember: “muy caro” is just a description; “demasiado caro” says it is a problem.
The dishes on the menu are very good.
The sixty-euro menu is too expensive for us: we can’t pay for it.
The terrace is much nicer than the dining room.
One by one? One more? The whole group?
Each person chooses their dish.
Do you have another free date?
All the colleagues sign the card.
Each guest brings a small present for Pilar.
There’s no room on Saturday. Do you have another free day?
Pilar knows all the colleagues at the office.
The wines on the list are too expensive.
Is there a vegetarian restaurant in the neighbourhood?
El Patio restaurant, good morning. Ramiro speaking.
Good morning. I’d like to book for Saturday, for sixteen people. Do you have a big table on the terrace?
I’m sorry, there isn’t a single free table left on the terrace on Saturday. But we have some big tables in the dining room.
And is the dining room quiet? In other restaurants there’s too much noise on Saturdays.
Yes, it’s very quiet and there’s a lot of space. For a big group it’s much better.
Perfect. And how much is the group menu?
Thirty-five euros. It includes a starter, a main course and dessert, and each person chooses their dish.
Very good. Some colleagues don’t eat meat. Is there a vegetarian dish?
Yes, there are lots of options: all the starters are vegetarian.
Great. And one more question: we’re going to bring a cake. Is that a problem?
No, no problem at all. But on Saturdays we’re very busy and we don’t have much time, so please arrive at nine o’clock sharp.
All right. So, a table for sixteen in the dining room, on Saturday at nine. Thank you very much!
Why doesn’t Lucía book on the terrace?
What is the dining room like, according to Ramiro?
Why does the group have to arrive at nine sharp?
Do you have any preference for dessert?
No, none. I like everything.
The waiters are very friendly.
But on Saturdays there are too many customers and the food takes a long time.
Sorry, I have a lot of work on Saturday. Shall we have another dinner next month?
Pilar works a lot and doesn’t sleep much.
Each person chooses their dessert.
The dining room is much quieter.
Why is Ramiro calling?
Why is there a free table on the terrace now?
What problem might the terrace have on Saturday night?
What about the vegetarian dishes?
When does Ramiro need the answer about the terrace?
exists or not; ninguno is almost always singular
they agree with the noun
with a verb or an adjective, only one form
one by one, one more, the whole group

Look at the word next to it. With a noun, quantity words agree: algún día, ninguna mesa, muchas personas, poca gente. With a verb or an adjective, they don’t change: trabaja mucho, muy caro, demasiado caros. And “muy” never stands alone.
There’s no cinema in my neighbourhood.
This week I have too many meetings: I have no time to eat.
My sister reads a lot: two books every week.
The train is much faster than the bus.
Do you have another pen? This one doesn’t work.
A month later, Pilar is living in another city and is looking for a flat. After a viewing, she writes her notes. Complete the sentences with the right quantity word.
To go further: cualquier (it doesn’t matter which), the difference between poco and un poco before an adjective, and a rare plural of ninguno.
“¿Tienen alguna mesa?” asks whether one exists. “Cualquier mesa está bien” says it doesn’t matter which one. Before a noun, masculine or feminine: cualquier. On its own or after the noun: cualquiera.
Any day is fine: I’m free all week.
Which table would you like? Any of them, thanks.
The room isn’t very bright: it only has one small window.
The menu is a bit expensive, but the food is excellent.
I don’t feel like cooking at all today: let’s go to the restaurant!

You can now say “No queda ninguna mesa” and “Ninguna mesa está libre”. In class 072 you work in depth on this double negative with nadie, nada and nunca: “No viene nadie”, “Nunca voy allí” or “No voy nunca”. It is the natural next step: you already know when you need “no” with ninguno; now you apply it to all negative words.

Marina Salgado and her friend Lorena rent an apartment in Cartagena, Colombia, for a week. They arrive on Friday at eleven at night. But there is nobody at the front desk, there is nothing in the kitchen and in the second bedroom there are no towels and no sheets. Today you learn to say everything that isn’t there, that doesn’t work and that never happens.
“No hay nadie en la portería” means…
The opposite of “siempre” is…
The fridge is empty: there’s nothing.
Does the negative word come after the verb?
Last night nobody came to open the door.
Lorena didn’t eat anything on the plane.
I never drink coffee at night.
There’s no mirror in the bathroom.
In a one-word answer, the negative word alone is enough: “Nadie”, “Nada, gracias”, “Nunca”. With a verb, “no” comes back: “No, no quiero nada”.
When they arrived, there was nobody at the front desk.
Lorena doesn’t know anybody in Cartagena.
We didn’t see anybody in the street.
Does the negative word come before the verb?
Nobody answered the phone at the front desk.
I never go to the beach at midday: it’s very hot.
None of the windows closes properly.
I never go there.
Nobody opened the door for me.
Federico never reads messages at night.
“No voy nunca allí” and “Nunca voy allí”…
Are you saying “same as you”?
—I’m hot. —Me too.
—I’m not sleepy. —Me neither.
The wifi doesn’t work and the TV doesn’t either.
Are you denying two things at once?
In the bedroom there are neither towels nor sheets.
Neither Marina nor Lorena slept well.
—I don’t know Cartagena. —Me neither.
—I love this neighbourhood. —Me too.
In the kitchen there’s neither coffee nor sugar.
Which sentence is correct?
—I don’t want to go out tonight. —Me neither.
Good morning, Marina. How did it go last night? Is everything OK with the apartment?
Good morning, Federico. Well… not very well. We arrived at eleven and there was nobody at the front desk.
How strange! The doorman never leaves before midnight. And the keys?
They were in the key box, luckily. But in the second bedroom there are no towels and no sheets.
Oh, I’m very sorry. And in the kitchen? I always leave coffee and water for guests.
This time there’s nothing. And the wifi cuts out every five minutes.
The wifi? We never have problems with the wifi. And the air conditioning?
The air conditioning doesn’t work well either: it makes a lot of noise. Lorena didn’t sleep at all, and neither did I.
I’m really sorry. Nobody told me. Today at twelve a technician is coming, and I’ll bring you towels, sheets and coffee.
Thank you very much. One more question: is there a supermarket nearby? We don’t know anybody in the neighbourhood.
Yes, there’s one on the corner. Do you need anything else?
No, nothing else, thanks. Bye.
What happened when Marina and Lorena arrived?
What does Federico say about the wifi?
How did Marina and Lorena sleep?
We arrived late and nobody opened the door for us.
In my room there wasn’t a single towel.
This morning we didn’t have anything for breakfast: the fridge was empty.
Federico says the doorman never misses work.
Today it isn’t raining at all: let’s go to the beach!
Nobody came to clean.
We never leave the door open.
Neither the TV nor the wifi works.
Lorena didn’t talk to anybody on the beach.
What is the main idea?
What was wrong with the wifi?
Why were there no towels or sheets?
Where are the towels and the coffee now?
Why didn’t the doorman see anybody last night?
after the verb: “no” is required
before the verb: no “no”
to say “same”, look at the other sentence
denies two things at once

Look at where the negative word is. After the verb: put “no” before the verb (“No vino nadie”). Before the verb: no “no” (“Nadie vino”). With people, “a nadie” (“No vi a nadie”). And to agree with something negative, “tampoco”, never “también no”.
Yesterday my phone was silent all day: nobody called me.
My brother never eats vegetables.
—I don’t like horror films. —Me neither.
There’s no pharmacy on this street.
This month I have neither the time nor the money to travel.
Back home, Lorena starts a new job. Her first day is a bit sad. Change the positive sentences into negative ones, as Lorena says them.

An extra step, if you have time. In Spanish you can put several negative words together in one sentence: “Nunca le digo nada a nadie” (I never tell anybody anything). The word “sin” works like a negative: “Se fue sin decir nada” (he left without saying anything). And “jamás” means the same as “nunca”, but stronger.
With a verb or an adjective, “no… nada” means “not at all”: “No me gusta nada”, “El apartamento no es nada caro”, “Lorena no durmió nada”.
Lorena left the party without saying anything.
“Este apartamento no es nada caro” means…
Marina is very discreet: she never tells anybody anything.

You can now say what isn’t there, what doesn’t work and what never happens: “No había nadie”, “Nunca voy allí”, “Yo tampoco”. In class 073 you go back out into the street: you learn to say which way you go and where things are, with prepositions like hacia, por, hasta, entre or enfrente de. It’s the natural next step: after complaining about the apartment, you go out to explore the city and explain how to get places.

Elena Soto leads bike tours. This Saturday her group leaves from the old station and goes as far as lago Azul. First they go towards the north and pass through two tunnels. Raúl Méndez is new in the group and has lots of questions: which way do we go? where do we stop? where is the van? Today you learn the prepositions for moving and for placing things.
We are going towards the north.
We go through the tunnel.
The group is opposite the station.
“Vamos hacia el norte”: what does “hacia” say?
“Pasamos por el túnel” means…
Which sentence is about a fixed place, with no movement?
Where are you going? In which direction? How far?
At eleven we arrive in the village.
Then we go towards the north, along the river.
We keep going as far as the lake and we eat there.
Where do you leave from? Which way do you go?
We set off from the old station to the lake.
From the village to the lake it is fifteen kilometres.
We go along the river path and through two tunnels.
The path ends at the bridge. We keep going as far as the bridge and stop there.
To get to the lake, we go through San Miguel.
Raúl comes to the station by metro.
Where exactly is it?
The lights are in the backpack.
The van is behind the café.
We eat between the beach and the bridge.

“Delante de la estación”: right by the door, on the same side of the street. “Enfrente de la estación”: on the other side of the street or the square, facing it. Elena says “El grupo está enfrente de la estación” because the cyclists wait on the other side of the street.
You can’t see the van from the street: it is behind the café.
The fountain is between the station and the church.
The lights are inside the backpack.
We are going to the lake.
We are heading towards the lake.
We go as far as the lake.

With “llegar”, the destination takes “a”: “Llegamos a San Miguel” (not “en San Miguel”). With “entrar” there is variation: “Entramos en el túnel” is common in Spain; “Entramos al túnel” is common in Latin America. Both are correct.
It is very foggy. We don’t know if we will get there, but we are heading towards the village.
This train doesn’t go to the centre: it only goes as far as Norte station. It ends there.
Elena and the group arrive at the lake at one o’clock.
Irene arrives at the station at a quarter to nine.
The helmet is on the table.
Hi, are you Elena? I’m Raúl, the new one. Do we set off from here?
Hi, Raúl! Yes, at nine. The group is over there, opposite the station, next to the fountain.
And where exactly are we going?
We go as far as lago Azul: it’s thirty-five kilometres. First we head north, along the river path.
Is it hard?
No, it’s almost flat. But we go through two tunnels and inside the tunnels there is no light. Do you have lights?
Yes, they’re in my backpack. Is there a stop?
Yes. At eleven we arrive in San Miguel, a small village. Gabriel waits for us there with the van, behind the café.
And where do we eat?
At the lake, under the trees, between the beach and the bridge. And at five we come back by train.
Perfect! Then I’ll leave my bike with the group.
Yes, leave it in front of the fountain: first we take a group photo.
Estar + **en**: el lugar general donde está algo, sin movimiento (in).
Where is the group waiting?
Why does Raúl need lights?
How do they get back home?
I come from Valdeluz, a village ten kilometres away.
Today I’m coming by bike, but I usually come by bus.
The river path goes towards the north.
Gabriel drives through the village centre to get to the square.
The cyclists arrive in San Miguel at eleven.
We set off from the station to the lake.
The van is next to the church.
We go through two dark tunnels.
The fountain is between the church and the bar.
What is the main idea?
Where is the meeting point?
Which way do they go tomorrow?
Where does Gabriel wait with the van?
How do they get back from the lake?
the starting point; desde pairs well with hasta
do you arrive, just head that way, or stop there?
the place you go through or along; how you travel
a fixed place, no movement

First look at the verb: is there movement, or is it a fixed place? With movement you choose the point: desde (start), por (path), hacia (direction), hasta (end), a (destination). Without movement: en, or a phrase with de (detrás de, enfrente de). And don’t forget: “llegar a”, “pasar por”.
The bank is between the chemist’s and the bakery.
To get to the centre, you go over the new bridge.
We walked towards the beach, but we didn’t get there: it started to rain.
The keys are not on the table: they are under the table, on the floor.
Tomorrow my sister arrives in Bogotá by plane.
A month later, Raúl organises a walking route through the old town of his city for some friends. Help him write the instructions: join the sentences.
We ride a lap around the lake: it’s six kilometres.
There are benches to rest all along the river.
I don’t know the exact time: we’ll arrive at about two.
The trail crosses the park: it goes through the gardens.

Today you used “por” for the path: “Pasamos por el túnel”. In class 074 you meet more uses of “por” and compare it with “para”: “Trabajo para Ana”, “Cambio el turno por ti”. It is the natural next step: you already know which way you go; now you learn to say why and for whom.

Pablo works at La Espiga, a bakery with a café. The owner is Ana Ruiz. On Saturday Pablo can’t work: his sister is getting married. His colleague Lucía helps him. Read what they say: they both use para and por.
Pablo: “I work for Ana.” Ana is his boss: his work goes to her.
Lucía: “I’ll swap the shift for you.” Pablo is the reason: she does it because he needs it.
Para looks ahead: the goal, the destination, the person who receives something, the deadline. Por looks back or along the way: the cause, the place you go through, the time of day, what you pay.
“Trabajo para Ana” means…
“Cambio el turno por ti” means…
What for? Where to?
Pablo asks for Saturday off to go to the wedding.
Lucía goes to the shop to buy a present.
On Friday Pablo leaves for Valencia.
The bus to Valencia leaves at six.
For whom? By when?
This coffee is for the lady at table two.
We want a present for Marta.
Ana needs the new rota by Thursday.
Lucía goes to the market to buy fruit.
These cakes are for the party at the office across the street.
I need the boxes by eleven, please.
Why? Because of what?
Pablo isn’t working on Saturday because of his sister’s wedding.
Today we are closing early because of a fault in the oven.
Thanks for the swap. Thanks for coming.
Which way? Roughly when? For how much?
Lucía stops by the shop before work.
Is there a pharmacy around here?
Pablo leaves in the afternoon.
We bought three cups for thirty euros.
The bus is late because of the traffic.
Every day I go to work through the park: it’s nicer.
I’m selling my bike for a hundred euros.
I’m not working because of the wedding.
I’m not working because my sister is getting married.
Pablo is nervous because he has to speak at the wedding.
Pablo is nervous because of the wedding.
Thank you very much for your help with the rota.
Lucía is saving money to travel in the summer.
Lucía, have you got a minute? I want to ask you a favour.
Sure. What’s up?
I can’t work on Saturday because of my sister Marta’s wedding. It’s in Valencia.
How nice! And when are you leaving for Valencia?
On Friday afternoon. I’m going by bus.
Don’t worry, I’ll swap the shift for you. I’ll give you my Tuesday for your Saturday: I work on Saturday and you work next Tuesday.
Perfect! Thanks so much for doing it.
You’re welcome. But Ana needs the new rota by Thursday. I’ll tell her today.
All right. She always sends out the rotas on Friday.
Another thing: Ana and I want to buy a present for Marta.
How thoughtful! There’s a pottery shop around here, on the street behind. They sell lovely cups for about ten euros.
Great. Tomorrow I’ll stop by the shop to look at the cups.
Why can’t Pablo work on Saturday?
Which day does Pablo work instead of Lucía?
Why is Lucía stopping by the shop tomorrow?
Today we are closing an hour early because of a fault.
This white coffee is for the lady by the window.
The train to Madrid leaves at ten past nine.
Pablo comes to work through the square: it’s shorter.
Ana needs the invoices by Monday at the latest.
I’ve been working for Ana for two years.
I’ll swap the shift for you.
Pablo leaves for Valencia in the afternoon.
Thanks for the present for my sister.
What is the main idea?
By when does Ana need the new rota?
Why are they opening at eight on Saturday?
How much did Ana pay for the cups?
Why are they taking the cups to the bakery?
why? the reason, what comes first
which way? roughly when? for how much?
what for? where to?
for whom? by when?
Ask the question first. What for, where to, for whom, by when? → para. Why, which way, roughly when, for how much? → por. And remember: por + noun, porque + verb; always gracias por.
The road is closed because of the snow.
These muffins are for the neighbour’s children.
Tomorrow I leave for Bogotá at seven.
Thanks for waiting for me.
Is there a cash machine around here?
On Friday, Pablo is at the bus station. Write each idea with por or para.

Optional. Por also says how you send or receive something: by phone, by email, by message. And it appears in fixed expressions: por favor, por fin (at last), por ejemplo, por supuesto (of course). Para mí gives your opinion: “In my opinion, Saturday is the best day.” In class 105 (B1) you will see more differences, like “lo hice por ti” and “lo hice para ti”.
Ana sends the rota to the whole team by email.
At last Pablo’s bus is leaving! It was an hour late.
In my opinion, the wedding was beautiful. What about you?
Lucía talks to Pablo on the phone on Sunday.

You can now explain why, what for and for whom you do something: “No trabajo por la boda”, “El regalo es para Marta”. In class 075 you go back to describing people, but now what changes: “es alto”, “hoy está muy elegante”, “lleva un traje azul”. It is the natural next step: Marta’s wedding is coming, and to talk about it you need to describe the people on that day.

Marta lives in Valencia. Today her friend Raúl arrives from Seville by train. Marta has a meeting, so her partner Hugo is going to pick him up at the station. But Hugo has never met Raúl. How will he recognise him? Marta describes him with three verbs: ser, estar and llevar.
Raúl is tall and blond.
Today he is a bit tired.
He wears glasses and has a beard.
“Raúl es alto” is about…
“Hoy está un poco cansado” is about…
Raúl wears glasses.
What is he / she like? (characteristics)
Raúl is tall, blond and very nice.
Hugo is short and quite serious.
How is he / she now? How does he / she look today?
After the trip, Raúl is tired.
You look so slim! Do you run a lot?
Marta, you look really nice today.
Hugo doesn’t know Raúl. Marta explains: “Raúl is tall and blond”.
Marta sees a new photo of Raúl: “He looks so slim!”
What is he / she wearing? (clothes, accessories, hair)
Raúl wears glasses and has a beard.
Now he wears his hair very short.
Today he is wearing a green jacket.

Body features you can’t change go with tener or ser: “Tiene los ojos verdes”, “Es alto”. Clothes and glasses go with llevar: “Lleva una chaqueta”. With hair and beards both are correct: “Tiene barba” / “Lleva barba”. With “lleva” you think more about how he looks now.
Raúl has green eyes.
Today Marta is wearing a blue dress.
Do you wear glasses for reading?
Raúl puts on his jacket.
Raúl is wearing his jacket on the train.

In Spain people say “gafas”. In many Latin American countries they say “lentes” or “anteojos”. And in many parts of Latin America “usar” is very common for something habitual: “Usa lentes” (he wears glasses), “Usa barba”. For today’s clothes, “llevar” is understood everywhere.
It’s cold. Hugo puts on his coat and leaves the house.
At the station, Hugo is wearing a grey coat.
Hugo is a bit nervous: he doesn’t know Raúl.
Raúl is nervous before arriving.
To recognise him: Raúl is carrying a black backpack.
Hey, what does your friend Raúl look like? I don’t know how to recognise him.
Well, he’s tall and blond, and he’s really nice. Look, this is a photo from university.
You look so young! Here he has long hair and a huge T-shirt.
Yes, but that was ten years ago. Now he has very short hair and a beard. Look, this one is from last week.
Let’s see… That’s true, he has changed a lot. And he’s slimmer, isn’t he?
Yes, he runs every day now. Oh, and he wears glasses: he didn’t before.
OK: tall, blond, beard and glasses. And what is he wearing today? There are lots of people at the station.
I don’t know. I’ll send him a message now and ask him.
And how is he? He’s coming from far away.
He’s a bit tired: he has been travelling for four hours. But he’s really happy to come.
Don’t worry, I’ll find him. By the way, you look really nice today. Is it for the meeting?
Thanks! Yes, today I’m wearing my blue dress: it’s an important meeting.
What is different about Raúl now?
Why doesn’t Marta know what Raúl is wearing today?
How is Raúl today, according to Marta?
There’s a guy here who is tall and blond, but he isn’t wearing glasses.
Another guy is wearing a red cap and has a suitcase.
A woman is very nervous: her train leaves in two minutes.
One more clue: Raúl has green eyes, like his mother.
Are you Raúl? Hi! I’m Hugo, Marta’s partner.
Raúl is tall, but today he is tired.
Marta is wearing a blue dress.
Now he has a beard and wears glasses.
You’ve changed so much!
Why does Raúl send the message?
What time does the train arrive?
What is Raúl wearing today?
What hasn’t changed about Raúl?
Why is he a bit tired?
characteristics: body, age, personality
a state now or a change you notice
clothes, accessories and hairstyle
body features you don’t put on

To describe a person, ask three questions. What is he like? → ser: “Es alto”. How is he now? → estar: “Está cansado”, “Está más delgado”. What is he wearing? → llevar: “Lleva gafas y una chaqueta verde”. Never “es con gafas” or “lleva los ojos verdes”.
My grandmother is very short and very cheerful.
I’m not going to class today: I’m ill.
In the wedding photo, my brother is wearing a grey suit.
Paula has curly hair and dark eyes.
You look so good in that shirt!
On Monday Marta leaves an envelope at a hotel reception desk for her colleague Ana. She describes Ana to the receptionist. Write Marta’s sentences.

Optional. With some adjectives, ser and estar change the meaning a lot: clever / ready, boring / bored, rich / tasty. And llevar has another use with time: “Raúl lleva tres años en Sevilla” (he has been in Seville for three years).
Dinner is ready: everyone to the table!
Raúl is very clever: he speaks four languages.
Hugo is bored: there’s nothing interesting on TV.
Mmm! This omelette tastes really good.
Raúl has been in Seville for three years: he loves the city.

You can now describe people with three verbs: “Es alto”, “Está cansado”, “Lleva gafas”. In class 076 you move from people to rules and instructions: “Aquí se habla español”, “¿Cómo se dice…?”, “Se compra el billete en la máquina”. It is the natural next step: you can describe the people you see at the station; now you learn to explain how things are done, without saying who does them.

Elena Duarte runs a small hostel in Santa Marta, on the coast of Colombia: La Ceiba. Hugo Ramírez is the new receptionist. Today they are making the reception signs and the breakfast menu. On signs, in recipes and in instructions, Spanish uses one form a lot: se + verb.
On the sign “Bikes for rent”, who rents out the bikes?
“No smoking in the rooms” is…
Se + verb in the 3rd person: we talk about the action, not about who does it. Typical of recipes, signs, manuals and rules.
First, the onion is chopped. / First, you chop the onion.
Reception closes at midnight.
How do you say “towel” in Spanish?
In class 031 you saw “Hugo se levanta a las seis”: there is a specific person (Hugo) and the action goes back to him. In “Se corta la cebolla” there is no person: it is a general instruction.
Which sentence is a general instruction, for everyone?
Nadia doesn’t know a word: “How do you say ‘pillow’ in Spanish?”
The verb agrees with the thing: one thing → singular verb; several things → plural verb (-n). The thing can go before or after the verb.
The onion is chopped and the tomatoes are chopped.
Coffee from the mountains for sale.
Towels are changed every three days.
Hostel menu: “Fresh juices for sale.”
Recipe: “First, mix the flour with water.”
Sign: “Keys are left at reception.” / “Leave keys at reception.”
Rules and permission: se puede (it is allowed / possible) and no se puede (it is not allowed), followed by an infinitive. With an infinitive alone, or with no thing at all, the verb is singular.
Smoking is not allowed in the rooms.
Can I pay by card? / Is paying by card possible?
You can eat on the terrace, but not in the kitchen.

Sometimes several things come after the infinitive: “Se pueden alquilar bicicletas en recepción.” The plural is the most recommended form, but you will also hear “se puede alquilar bicicletas”. In this class we use se puede with the infinitive alone (se puede pagar, no se puede entrar).
Pool sign: “No swimming after nine.”
Nadia asks: “Can guests use the kitchen at night?”
Elena is chopping the onion in the kitchen.
Hugo, chop the onion, please.
The onion is chopped into small pieces.
Elena writes the recipe on the kitchen board: “Grate the cheese.”
Elena talks to Hugo, who is next to her: “Hugo, open the door, please.”
Hostel shop sign: “Caps and hats for sale.”
“Dogs are not allowed on the beach.” (lit. you can’t go in with dogs)
Hugo, today we’re making the new signs. The first one is easy: “Spanish spoken here.”
Shall I also put “Bikes for rent”? We’ve got six new ones now.
Yes, of course. And another one for the rooms: “No smoking.”
And can people smoke on the terrace?
On the terrace, yes. Now, the menu. Look at the arepa recipe: first you mix the flour with warm water and salt.
And the cheese? They’re cheese arepas, aren’t they?
Yes. You put a little grated cheese in the dough. Then you shape the arepas with your hands.
And how long do you leave them on the griddle?
About five minutes on each side. And remember: coffee is served on the terrace, not in the kitchen.
Good morning. Excuse me, can I pay by card here?
Yes, of course, by card or in cash. And if you want a bike, bikes are returned before eight in the evening.
Perfect! And I see the sign: Spanish spoken here. All the better for practising!
Where can people smoke at the hostel?
What goes into the arepa dough?
When are the bikes returned?
Beach towels for rent.
Breakfast is served from seven to ten.
No loud music after eleven at night.
First, cut the lemons in half.
How do you say “to squeeze” in Spanish?
Spanish spoken here.
No smoking in the rooms.
The arepas are served with butter.
Bikes for rent at reception.
Elena gives Hugo instructions with tú. Now Hugo writes them in the recipe for everyone, with no person.
What is the main idea?
Why is Hugo making breakfast?
What is mixed with the flour?
How long are the arepas cooked?
Why don’t guests have breakfast in the kitchen?
one thing, or no thing at all → singular verb
several things, before or after the verb → plural verb (-n)
rules and permission: singular with the infinitive
when it matters who: command or a named subject

For recipes, rules and signs: se + 3rd-person verb, it doesn’t matter who. Then look at the thing: one → se corta; several → se cortan. With an infinitive alone or with no thing, singular: se puede fumar, se cena a las ocho.
Shop sign: “Second-hand clothes for sale.”
Coffee machine manual: “First, put water in the tank.”
Museum sign: “No food allowed inside.”
Recipe: “Cook the potatoes in salted water for twenty minutes.”
Ad: “Room with bathroom for rent, near the beach.”
Marcos works at a public library. His boss gives him notes with tú; he writes the rules for all the readers, with se.

In recipes and on signs you will see three styles: the command for one person (“Corta la cebolla”), se for everyone (“Se corta la cebolla”) and the infinitive, very common in written recipes and on short signs (“Cortar la cebolla”, “No fumar”). On formal signs you will also see “Se prohíbe fumar” (smoking is prohibited). All three are correct; when speaking, people normally use the command or se.

You can now explain how something is done: “First the flour is mixed… then the arepas are shaped.” To order the steps better and explain why, you need connectors: first, then, finally, that’s why. In class 077 you learn to link the ideas of a recipe, a trip or a day. It is the natural next step: you have the steps, now you connect them.
